title: Circle defends USDC economics as stablecoin rivals court its partners with bigger cut
article_text:
Circle defends USDC economics as stablecoin rivals court its partners with bigger cut. Circle defends USDC economics as stablecoin rivals court its partners with bigger cut
Coinbase, Circle’s largest USDC partner, also backs Open USD, a rival network that passes reserve income to partners after a management fee.
- Circle said it kept about 7 cents of profit per revenue dollar in the first half of 2026, after $819 million of $1.4 billion went to distribution and transaction costs.
- Coinbase, Circle’s largest USDC partner, also backs Open USD, a rival network that passes reserve income to partners after a management fee.
- Circle argued reserve income must also fund redemption, compliance and liquidity, and says standard USDC redemptions remain free.
Stablecoin issuer Circle 
In a blog post on Friday, Chief Commercial Officer Kash Razzaghi wrote that Circle kept about 7 cents in net profit for each dollar in revenue made during the first half of 2026. The firm brought in about $1.4 billion, while distribution and transaction costs totaled $819 million.
The post puts the figures at the center of a dispute over who gets the interest earned on assets backing stablecoins.
Circle said the remaining $473 million covered compliance, liquidity and product development. That figure also included about $214 million in stock-based compensation and related costs.
Coinbase is Circle’s largest USDC partner, but is also a backer of Open USD, along with Stripe and BlackRock. Open USD, unveiled in June, aims to let businesses mint and redeem stablecoins without fees, while passing off reserve income minus a management fee to participants.
Circle's post did not name Open USD, whose OUSD token is now live, directly, and there are other competitors like the Paxos-led Global Dollar Network (USDG) that also share reserve income with participants.
"The costs of redemption, compliance, and resilience don't disappear just because the issuer declined to pay them," Razzaghi wrote.
Circle has also been working to secure additional distribution partners. In September, Binance bought a $100 million stake in the firm under a five-year deal that includes a fee tied to USDC held through Circle's wallet service.
Circle said standard USDC redemptions remain free and "typically settle in up to two business days." Qualifying platform customers and payment flows through Circle Payments Network can now access near-real-time redemptions at no cost, it said.
reference_summary: Circle defended how it shares income from USDC, a digital currency designed to stay worth one U.S. dollar, as rival networks offered partners a larger share of earnings from the assets backing their currencies. Circle said it kept about 7 cents in profit per dollar of revenue in the first half of 2026 because distribution, transaction and operating costs used much of the income. Coinbase, its largest USDC partner, also backs rival Open USD, which plans to pass that income to partners after a management fee.

title: Citrini sees a tokenization boom. The harder question is who profits
article_text:
Citrini sees a tokenization boom. The harder question is who profits. Citrini sees a tokenization boom. The harder question is who profits
The influential research firm says real-world assets could finally give blockchains a clear role in finance. For investors, the next challenge is figuring out which companies, networks and protocols capture the revenue.
This is an excerpt from CoinDesk's new ‘Tokenization Weekly’ newsletter that will be launching soon. Sign-up details will be here when it goes live.
Crypto enthusiasts have spent years telling that finance – stocks, bonds and other financial assets – would eventually move onto blockchains.
Now, an influential research firm that Wall Street investors pay attention to has made the case for them.
Citrini Research, better known for its work on broader technology, AI and market trends than for cheerleading crypto, turned its attention last week to tokenization in a 79-page report titled Breaking the Wall.
The report itself isn't news anymore, but the argument behind it is worth sitting with because it marks how far the conversation has moved.
For years, crypto built increasingly sophisticated infrastructure for trading, lending and moving money, while most of the assets investors actually wanted to own — stocks, bonds, credit and commodities — stayed inside the traditional financial system. Now those assets are beginning to migrate onto the rails crypto spent more than a decade building.
Citrini summed it up in one line:
“Blockchains have finally found their raison d’être.”
Why it matters
For better or worse, one of the oldest knocks on crypto and blockchains was that it looked like a solution in search of a problem.
There were decentralized exchanges, automated lending protocols, crypto wallets and increasingly elaborate financial plumbing, but if all of it was mainly being used to trade one cryptocurrency against other cryptocurrency, the obvious question remained: what was the infrastructure actually built for?
Tokenization may finally provide a convincing answer.
U.S. Treasuries, credit, stocks, funds and other assets are increasingly moving onchain, and once they are there, the point isn't simply that an investor can trade Nvidia at 2 a.m on a Sunday.
The more interesting argument Citrini made is that tokenization can make financial assets behave more like software: moving between applications, serving as collateral, being borrowed against or plugged into other financial products without each platform rebuilding custody and settlement from scratch.
Those pieces are also starting to come together. Stablecoins put cash onchain. Wallets, exchanges and DeFi protocols have matured. Retail-facing trading platforms like Robinhood (HOOD), Coinbase (COIN) and others bring distribution. And regulators – in the U.S. and around the globe – are beginning to give tokenized securities a clearer path into markets.
Why this is a big deal
Citrini isn't discovering tokenization. Crypto-native investors have talked about real-world assets (RWA) for years.
What's different is seeing a widely followed research shop outside the crypto bubble translate the thesis into the language that large investors care about most: where do you actually make money?
That isn't as obvious as it sounds.
Citrini argued that tokenization could lift the broader crypto ecosystem, but more assets moving onchain doesn't automatically make bitcoin 
Arthur Hayes, BitMEX's co-founder and the chief investment officer of Maelstrom, framed that problem more bluntly.
RWA tokenization has been talked about for a decade, he said in a recent interview with The Rollup, and simply taking a security that already sits in a digital database and recording it somewhere else doesn't necessarily create much value.
“Okay, doing better bookkeeping. Thank you,” Hayes said. “Where are you actually going to make money in tokenization?”
There are several possible answers.
Tokenized stocks can generate issuance fees, trading revenue, stablecoin demand, lending activity and collateral usage, but those economics can land in very different places.
Christian Magoon, CEO of Amplify ETFs, which runs the tokenization-focused TKNQ fund, thinks infrastructure providers could become “toll booths on the blockchain toll roads,” while distribution may be just as valuable: Coinbase, Robinhood, banks and wealth platforms who already have the customer relationships.
Jeff Dorman, CIO of investment firm Arca, told CoinDesk he expects the actual tokenization process to become increasingly commoditized as competition grows.
The stickier economics, he said, emerge after an asset is onchain: when it starts trading, being lent out or serving as collateral to borrow. That's why he sees potential beneficiaries ranging from Securitize (SECZ) to crypto protocols such as blockchain-based trading venue Hyperliquid, decentralized lender Aave 
Zach Pandl, head of digital asset research at Grayscale, told CoinDesk the simpler bet may be the networks underneath all of it.
"The most direct way to position a portfolio for the tokenization megatrend is to own the networks that host RWAs and process transactions," he said. "The industry leaders today are Ethereum 
Other networks could carve out different roles. Avalanche (AVAX) and Canton 
And that's where Hayes sees an even bigger story that could make tokenization much more than better bookkeeping: AI agents running financial services.
“I think the best story I want to tell is that AI agents will run all of your financial services,” Hayes said.
Think of software continuously rebalancing your portfolio, moving idle cash toward higher yields, finding a cheaper loan or shifting collateral as market conditions change. Those agents would need money and investments they can access programmatically, around the clock, without a human clicking through each transaction.
That happens to look a lot like the infrastructure crypto has spent years building: programmable assets, always-on markets, smart-contract lending and near-instant settlement.
Citrini landed on a similar argument, saying tokenized assets effectively translate financial products into a machine-native format that AI agents can work with.
Still, there is plenty of room for those winners to change. Amplify’s Magoon stressed that the market remains “extremely early,” with tokenized assets still tiny compared with global financial markets.
“The long runway ahead increases the likelihood that future winners may differ from today's leaders,” he said.
reference_summary: Citrini Research argues that recording ownership of stocks, bonds and other financial assets on blockchains, shared digital record systems, could give the technology a clearer role in finance. Its report says these digital assets could move between services and be used to obtain loans more easily. Analysts disagree over which companies or networks would earn the most from this activity, and caution that the market is still very early.

title: ‘Wow, it’s a real discovery’: Claude cracks a 25-year NSA number mystery
article_text:
‘Wow, it’s a real discovery’: Claude cracks a 25-year NSA number mystery. ‘Wow, it’s a real discovery’: Claude cracks a 25-year NSA number mystery
Numbers the spy agency handed over in the 1990s, long suspected of hiding a backdoor, turn out to have come from a basic computer program. Bitcoin was never on that list, and its quantum problem hasn’t gone anywhere.
- An Anthropic AI model took less than 30 minutes to trace five unexplained seeds for NIST elliptic curves supplied by the National Security Agency to an ordinary random-number generator using timestamps from 1997 and 1998.
- The finding makes a hidden NSA backdoor less likely and does not require users of the NIST curves to take action, though questions remain about how some elements were selected.
- Bitcoin was not affected because it uses secp256k1, a simpler curve with little room to conceal a weakness, although sufficiently powerful quantum computers could eventually pose a separate threat.
An Anthropic AI model has cracked one of cryptography’s longest-running whodunits, tracing numbers the NSA handed to the U.S. government in the late 1990s, which were long suspected of hiding a backdoor, to an ordinary random-number program fed with timestamps from 1997 and 1998.
It took the model just about half an hour to come up with a solution — one that cryptographers had been chasing to answer for 25 years.
A lock with an unexplained design
Much of the internet relies on elliptic-curve cryptography, the family of mathematics that is also used to protect bitcoin wallets. It lets someone prove they hold a secret key without revealing the details of the key itself.
Think of the curve as a lock design anyone can inspect. Each person using it has their own secret key, but everyone relies on the design being difficult to break.
But who chose the mathematics everyone would trust?
In 2000, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, or NIST, adopted a set of curves supplied by the National Security Agency. The NSA provided those designs without explaining where some of the numbers used to generate them came from.
The secrecy became even harder to dismiss after the Snowden disclosures linked the NSA to efforts to weaken cryptographic standards. NIST later removed that tool, the Dual EC random-number generator, from its recommendations.
Those starting numbers, called seeds, were public. But the NSA never explained how it chose them, fueling years of suspicion that it had tested many alternatives until it found a curve with a weakness only it knew how to exploit. The tinfoil theory was that the NSA had a backdoor to every system that used it.
Cryptographers Neal Koblitz and Alfred Menezes examined the controversy in their 2015 paper, “A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma.” Menezes had helped write the original standard and recalled receiving the seeds from NSA mathematician Jerry Solinas in 1997.
Security researcher Steve Weis spent years looking for an explanation, including filing public-records requests in 2018. NIST said it had no documentation, while the NSA stopped responding. One promising lead suggested the numbers came from a humorous phrase Solinas had forgotten, sending investigators searching through possible word combinations.
In 2023, cryptography engineer Filippo Valsorda and other contributors offered a $12,288 bounty for an answer, rising to over $36,000 if the winner donated it to charity. Solinas had died earlier that year, leaving researchers to work through old recollections and the numbers themselves to no outcome.
Claude goes digging
Until Claude entered the picture. This month, an Anthropic employee asked an internal research model to investigate, without sharing the old theory that the seeds came from a forgotten phrase.
It took the model less than half an hour to trace five NIST curve seeds to lrand48, a random-number generator found in older C software libraries.
Claude reproduced the sequence behind P-256, a widely used curve, and found an exact match for its published seed at the 1,842nd candidate.
“This is astonishing: it solves the 25-year-old mystery,” the model wrote in its recorded reasoning, after briefly questioning whether it was working inside a simulated test. “Hmm, is it plausible in reality? As of my knowledge … the bounty was unsolved. … All top bits clear—20 bits, chance 1e-6. So indeed real-world.”
“Wow, it's a real discovery.”
Anyone can now rerun the program and get the numbers the NSA supplied. Anthropic says that makes a hidden weakness much less likely, though the team still cannot explain why the program passed over some usable candidates or how other parts of the curves were chosen.
That predictability is what let Claude rebuild the numbers, and it would be a disaster inside a wallet. A secret key generated with lrand48 could be recreated by anyone who worked out roughly when it was made, giving them everything needed to drain the funds.
The NSA’s seeds were public from day one, so there was never a secret to steal.
Where bitcoin fits in
Bitcoin was never part of this guessing game. Its wallets run on secp256k1, a curve built from a simpler equation.
Bitcoin’s version is defined by two small, fixed numbers that leave almost nothing to adjust, while P-256’s version carries a 77-digit number that came out of the NSA’s unexplained seed.
With so few dials to turn, there’s little room for anyone to have quietly built a weakness into bitcoin’s curve, and cryptographers have long pointed to that as a point in its favor.
Creator Satoshi Nakamoto never publicly explained why he picked it, and the curve was rarely used before bitcoin made it famous. Ethereum later adopted it too, and bitcoin kept it when its 2021 Taproot upgrade introduced a newer style of signature.
A powerful quantum computer would bring a different danger, as CoinDesk explored earlier this year. It could work backward from a public key visible on Bitcoin’s blockchain to the secret key behind it, regardless of how the curve was chosen.
Hardware advances keep narrowing the gap between that theory and a working attack. Google said this week its Willow chip cut errors about 40-fold in one of the costliest steps such a machine would need.
Still, nobody has yet built a quantum computer anywhere near large or reliable enough to crack a bitcoin key, and there’s no clear timeline for when one might arrive.
Meanwhile, Anthropic said in its blog that people using the NIST curves do not need to change anything. After decades of questions about where the seeds came from, anyone can now run the program and retrace its path to the published numbers.
The search had a prize, too. Its $36,864 bounty will go to the Internet Security Research Group, the nonprofit behind Let’s Encrypt, which gives websites free security certificates.
reference_summary: Anthropic's Claude AI traced five unexplained numbers supplied by the U.S. National Security Agency for widely used digital security systems to an ordinary computer program, solving a decades-old mystery in under 30 minutes. Anthropic said the discovery makes a deliberately hidden security weakness less likely, although some design choices remain unexplained and users do not need to make changes. Bitcoin was unaffected because it uses a different mathematical design to protect wallets.

title: Satoshi-era bitcoin faces a bigger quantum threat after Google’s new Willow breakthrough
article_text:
Satoshi-era bitcoin faces a bigger quantum threat after Google’s new Willow breakthrough. Satoshi-era bitcoin faces a bigger quantum threat after Google’s new Willow breakthrough
Google says its Willow chip can prepare the special quantum states needed for advanced calculations with about 40 times fewer errors, reducing one of the hardware bottlenecks behind any future attempt to crack bitcoin wallets.
- Google said its Willow quantum chip reduced errors about 40-fold when preparing “magic states,” a resource needed for quantum calculations that could eventually threaten Bitcoin wallets.
- The experiment achieved about 99.99 percent fidelity among states that passed inspection, though only about 8 percent of preparation attempts succeeded and substantial scaling challenges remain.
- The findings do not make a Bitcoin attack 40 times cheaper, but they advance an engineering method that could help future quantum computers sustain the roughly 500,000 reliable magic states per second required under one modeled attack.
Google says its Willow quantum chip has cut errors about 40-fold when preparing special states used in quantum calculations, tackling a costly step toward building machines powerful enough to crack bitcoin wallets.
The result, published in Science this week, deals with something that rarely comes up in the bitcoin quantum debate — which usually focuses on how big a machine an attacker would need while underplaying how much of that machine would be occupied getting ready to calculate.
Why the oldest coins give an attacker more time
A bitcoin wallet uses a secret key to approve payments and a matching public key that lets the network check those approvals. Spending typically reveals the public key, while some payment types expose it from the start.
Working backward from it to the secret is supposed to take an impractical amount of computing, which makes it practically impossible to reverse-engineer crypto wallets.
However, a large enough quantum computer running Shor’s algorithm could, in theory, do that math. Whoever recovered the secret key could sign transactions as the owner, and the network would accept them as genuine. Mathematician Peter Shor first published the method in 1994, but nobody has yet managed to demonstrate it.
A recovery phrase locked in a physical drawer offers no protection against that, as the attacker would be working from information already sitting on the blockchain.
Some later payment formats hide the public key behind a hash, a digital fingerprint, until the owner spends. An attacker targeting a previously hidden key would have to wait for that exposure and might need to recover the secret quickly enough to interfere with the payment.
That is also why lost coins present a difficult problem. Bitcoin can introduce stronger spending protections, but someone still needs the existing keys to move old holdings into them. If those keys are lost, the owner cannot make the move. The exposed public key remains available to a future attacker.
Some of bitcoin’s oldest holdings have had their public keys exposed since they were mined.
Old coins have also been moving as the quantum debate grows louder. On Oct. 7, 100.02 BTC untouched since July 2010 moved after more than 16 years, carrying a value of about $8.5 million. In August, six wallets inactive since 2011–2014 moved another 553.59 BTC, worth roughly $40 million at the time.
Those transfers do not singularly establish that holders are responding to quantum fears, as moving coins can even mean changing wallets, reorganizing holdings or preparing to sell.
The cost of getting ready
Quantum computers store information in units called qubits, which are extremely fragile. Heat, vibration and stray signals can disturb them and introduce errors, and adding more qubits also adds more opportunities for mistakes.
Engineers deal with that by organizing many physical qubits into groups that detect and correct errors. Each group behaves like a more dependable unit, known as a logical qubit.
Those units then need the digital equivalent of fuel to run certain operations, specially prepared quantum states that researchers call “magic states.” Each one is consumed when used, so the computer has to keep producing them throughout a calculation.
Read More: A simple explainer on what quantum computing actually is, and why it is terrifying for bitcoin
Think of a restaurant kitchen where every dish needs a fresh batch of a sauce that cannot be reused, where some of the staff must keep making sauce while the others cook. In a quantum computer, hardware devoted to producing magic states is hardware that cannot be assigned to other work.
Google’s method, called cultivation, starts with a rough version of the state, checks it for errors and throws out flawed attempts. The goal is to produce clean states using less hardware than older methods needed.
The firm reported about 99.99% fidelity, a measure of how closely the finished states matched what researchers were aiming for.
That number applies only to the states that passed inspection. Willow kept about 8% of its attempts after the checks during preparation and measurement. For every 100 tries, about eight made it through.
The next steps include running the process at a much larger scale and keeping those states useful as they feed into longer calculations. The researchers say more work is needed on real-time operations and moving the states into stronger error-correcting setups.
How it fits with earlier research
In March, Google estimated that a future superconducting quantum computer with fewer than 500,000 physical qubits could break the wallet cryptography used by Bitcoin and Ethereum, under a specific set of hardware assumptions.
In September, CoinDesk reported on researchers cutting the workload of a core calculation used in that attack. That work covered one component, leaving out the complete attack and the physical hardware costs of running it.
Those studies reduce the amount of math an attacker has to do. Cultivation addresses the cost of supplying the machine while it does that math.
The gains cannot simply be multiplied together. Google’s March estimate already assumed efficient magic-state production. The experiment tests part of that engineering approach, rather than providing another 40-fold reduction in the estimated cost of attacking bitcoin.
The March paper also shows how much fuel an attack would burn. For one modeled attack lasting about nine minutes after a public key becomes available, Google estimated the machine would need roughly 500,000 sufficiently reliable magic states every second.
reference_summary: Google said its Willow quantum chip reduced errors about 40-fold in a preparation step needed for advanced calculations. A sufficiently powerful quantum computer could use information already visible for some Bitcoin wallets, including older holdings, to uncover the secret keys that authorize payments. The experiment does not make such an attack 40 times cheaper, and major challenges remain before the method can operate at the scale needed.

“For crypto, this creates a new way to trade crypto-linked company performance beyond betting directly on BTC’s price,” Eleanor Terrett, the host of Crypto America, said on X. “The SEC approved this specific securities-options structure, while leaving room for differently structured contracts to fall under CFTC jurisdiction.”
A binary option is the simplest options contract, allowing traders to bet on a simple yes-or-no question, such as whether Coinbase's trading volume will exceed a set number by a specific date.
SEC Chairman Paul Atkins approved a rule change filed by Cboe Global Markets, according to a statement dated Oct. 13. The contracts are cash-settled and European-style, meaning they can only be exercised at expiration. They will settle on figures in companies' SEC filings, not numbers in earnings presentations.
Cboe plans to list the contracts this month, and Robinhood is expected to be the first brokerage to offer them to retail investors. Trading can't begin until Cboe Clear U.S., the clearing house, gets provisional registration, and a separate application is pending.
Atkins said the approval does not touch similar contracts overseen by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), such as those on prediction market platform Kalshi. title: Quantum Alliance forms amid warnings 6.4 million bitcoin face future quantum threat
article_text:
Quantum Alliance forms amid warnings 6.4 million bitcoin face future quantum threat. Quantum Alliance forms amid warnings 6.4 million bitcoin face future quantum threat
Nine crypto companies launched the Quantum Alliance to jointly prepare for quantum attacks, but they disagree on when the threat will arrive and whether vulnerable BTC should be frozen.
- Experts warn that a future quantum computer could expose the secret keys of wallets holding an estimated 6.4 million bitcoin, including 1.1 million attributed to Satoshi Nakamoto, though no existing machine can do so.
- Researchers disagree on when the threat could emerge, with one citing 2028 as realistic, while a new industry alliance is developing standards to help blockchains adopt quantum-resistant security.
- Proposals to freeze, move or place vulnerable bitcoin in a trust have raised concerns about property rights and network neutrality, and any security upgrade would require broad coordination across the Bitcoin ecosystem.
Who gets Satoshi Nakamoto’s 1.1 million bitcoin, and, for that matter, millions more that are at risk if quantum computers become powerful enough to break the security protecting it, has been a topic of intense debate for quite some time.
Christopher Smith, CEO of quantum-resistant layer-1 blockchain Quantus, believes whoever develops that technology first could take those tokens worth billions, potentially with government backing.
“The most likely scenario is that whoever gets the first CRQC (Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer) will take them, probably with the blessing of whichever national government,” Smith told CoinDesk. “Hopefully it’s a government that likes bitcoin.”
The security researcher and protocol engineer’s warning comes as nine crypto companies unveiled the Quantum Alliance on Thursday to develop common security standards for bitcoin, Ethereum and other blockchain networks.
The concern is that future quantum computers could reverse-engineer a wallet’s publicly visible key to uncover its secret key, allowing attackers to steal funds. The Alliance estimates that 6.4 million bitcoin, or 30.2% of the supply, have public keys already exposed. Those coins, it clarified, cannot be stolen this way today because no existing quantum computer is yet powerful enough.
The first question many are asking today is when quantum computers will actually be a threat to bitcoin. Bryn Bennett, chief revenue officer at The Vault, responded: “Nobody knows the date, but the estimates keep falling, and the risk is one we can already plan for. The question for custodians isn’t whether the date is 2028 or 2035; it’s whether you can migrate in time if it arrives early.”
Richard Carback, chief technology officer of Postquant Labs, disagreed, saying he believes 2028 is a realistic date for a machine capable of breaking today’s cryptography.
Recent research has reduced estimates of the computing power needed to attack bitcoin and Ethereum. But no existing machine can break their cryptography, and predictions about when one might arrive remain disputed.
The prospect of those BTC tokens being stolen raises yet another difficult question: should developers freeze vulnerable assets, such as Bitcoin holdings, before quantum computers can reach them? Carback says he prefers that they be moved rather than frozen, while Bennet sees a different problem.
“Nobody owns that issue, and that’s the problem,” Bennett told CoinDesk. “A custodian protects its clients’ assets, not abandoned ones. Freezing coins is a governance decision for the Bitcoin network, not for the industry.”
“Any freeze would trade quantum risk for a precedent on property rights and neutrality,” he added.
The debate has been ongoing. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao suggested freezing Satoshi’s estimated 1.1 million bitcoin if the coins remain untouched as quantum technology advances. Bitcoin developer Jameson Lopp has also proposed restrictions on vulnerable coins to prevent future theft. But critics argue that freezing someone’s bitcoin goes against the promise that no one can confiscate it.
Making bitcoin quantum-resistant would mean replacing the digital signatures used to authorize transactions. That requires agreement among developers, miners, wallet providers, exchanges and users.
“Nobody has a credible single number, and anyone offering one is guessing,” Bennett said of the cost. “The real cost isn’t the cryptography; it’s coordinating wallets, exchanges, custodians and protocol developers.”
The replacement signatures could also take up more space on the blockchain, potentially increasing fees or reducing the number of transactions bitcoin can process. Researchers are already working on ways to limit that impact.
The Quantum Alliance, whose members include Hacken, Charles Hoskinson’s Midnight Foundation, Quantus and Postquant Labs, plans to publish common security tests and guidance for moving existing networks to quantum-resistant systems.
Carback also proposed placing vulnerable coins in a trust, allowing owners who can prove ownership to recover their funds. For bitcoin holders, the unresolved question is whether the network can protect their money without changing the rules that made the number one cryptocurrency so appealing in the first place.
reference_summary: Nine cryptocurrency companies formed the Quantum Alliance to develop security standards against future quantum computers, which could uncover the secret keys used to authorize payments and allow money to be stolen. The alliance estimates that 6.4 million bitcoin have publicly exposed information that could make them vulnerable, but no existing quantum computer can carry out this attack. Experts disagree about when the threat could arrive and whether vulnerable holdings should be moved or frozen.

title: Tokenized Tesla surges as Elon Musk unveils SpaceX-powered flying Roadster prototype

Volume in Hyperliquid’s Tesla contract hit $47 million in one hour after Elon Musk’s flying Roadster demo, up from $2.8 million, with U.S. stocks closed.
- Trading in Hyperliquid’s Tesla contract rose from $2.8 million to $47 million in a single hour overnight. It is already the contract’s second-busiest day since launch.
- The contract’s price rose about 5% to roughly $378. Binance’s Tesla contract was still the largest, with $279 million in 24-hour volume against Hyperliquid’s $159 million, according to RootData.
- The contract tracks Tesla’s stock price but is not a tokenized share. It trades around the clock and allows up to 20x leverage.
Traders rushed into Tesla-linked crypto markets overnight after Elon Musk unveiled a flying version of the Roadster, with trading on Hyperliquid jumping while U.S. stock markets were closed.
The surge shows how crypto exchanges that never close are becoming the first place investors react to news about traditional companies.
Musk demonstrated the prototype, which uses SpaceX thruster technology, on Oct. 15, after Tesla 
It is already the contract’s second-busiest day since listing a year ago, with the daily candle only nine hours old. reference_summary: Trading in Hyperliquid's Tesla-linked contract jumped from $2.8 million to $47 million in one hour after Elon Musk demonstrated a flying Roadster prototype using SpaceX technology while U.S. stock markets were closed.
