title: Scammer gets scammed in Ledger spy-chip exploit, loses almost $5 million in bitcoin
article_text:
Scammer gets scammed in Ledger spy-chip exploit, loses almost $5 million in bitcoin. Scammer gets scammed in Ledger spy-chip exploit, loses almost $5 million in bitcoin
Chainalysis says a fraudster who tricked people through fake online jobs became one of the biggest victims of the compromised hardware wallets.
- A crypto scammer who made millions through fake online job offers lost more than $4.9 million in bitcoin after thieves compromised Ledger hardware wallets.
- Chainalysis said the scammer transferred proceeds from their scheme to three wallet addresses, from which attackers stole 60 bitcoin.
- The theft was linked to Ledger devices sold by Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis that contained unauthorized implants capable of transmitting wallet recovery information over a mobile network.
A crypto scammer who made millions tricking people by offering fake online jobs has fallen victim to another scam, losing bitcoin worth more than $4.9 million through compromised Ledger hardware wallets.
Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis said Thursday on X that the perpetrator had collected the bitcoin through a so-called task scam, in which people are initially paid to post fake product reviews or boost online sales. Then they are told their accounts have a negative balance and they must deposit their own money before they can withdraw their supposed earnings.
According to Chainalysis, the person behind the operation transferred the proceeds of the illegal activity to three Ledger wallet addresses, which thieves emptied, taking 60 BTC.
The incident adds a twist to the Ledger security breach involving devices sold by Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis. Investigators discovered unauthorized hardware implants capable of transmitting wallet recovery information over a mobile network, giving attackers access to the bitcoin stored on affected devices.
reference_summary: Chainalysis said a fraudster who collected cryptocurrency through fake online job offers lost 60 bitcoin, worth more than $4.9 million, to other thieves. The theft involved Ledger wallet devices sold by reseller CryptoBilis that had been secretly fitted with hardware to send attackers the recovery information needed to access the funds.

title: Live updates: Bitcoin dips to $81,000 as stocks slide, VIX soars ahead of Black Monday anniversary
article_text:
Live updates: Bitcoin dips to $81,000 as stocks slide, VIX soars ahead of Black Monday anniversary. VIX soars, Nasdaq sheds 2% ahead of 39-year anniversary of 1987's Black Monday market crash
Surely just a coincidence, but this coming Monday marks the 39-year anniversary of the Black Monday, October 19, 1987, stock market crash, when the S&P 500 plunged more than 20%.
That makes today the 39-year anniversary of the Friday before the 1987 crash. While not nearly as dramatic as the S&P 500’s 5% decline 39 years ago, the Nasdaq fell 2.15% today.
Alongside, the volatility index (VIX) — often referred to as the “fear gauge” — soared 22%.
Rumors were flying of someone or some group getting blown out of their positions, but nothing’s been confirmed just yet.
Bitcoin is off of its lows, but still down 1% over the past 24 hours at $81,500.
Stocks losses quickly double, with bitcoin attempting to decouple
The Nasdaq is at session lows a bit less than 90 minutes before the close of trading for the week, down 2.3%. The S&P 500 is down 1.25%.
What was a modestly negative day appears to have turned into a rout as oil prices quickly jumped about $3 per barrel over the past couple of hours. WTI crude is now up 3.8% to $101.70.
Government bonds — which benefitted earlier this week as money flowed into fixed income alongside declining stocks — aren’t seeing a bid today. The 10-year Treasury yield is near the day’s high at 5.112%.
After initially declining alongside stocks earlier on Friday, bitcoin is attempting to stabilize as equities add to losses this afternoon. It’s currently at $81,350, down 1% over the past 24 hours.
Crypto stocks slammed as oil surges, interest rates turn higher, and stocks slide
Rising slowly at first, the price of oil is headed straight up over the past few minutes, with WTI crude now up more than 3% on the day to a one-month high of $101 per barrel.
That’s up 16% over the past 10 days.
There are reports that Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline has been targeted in an attack.
U.S. government bond yields are responding; the 10-year Treasury is now higher by 3.5 basis points to 5.125% after earlier dipping to 5.07%.
The Nasdaq is lower by 1.5% and bitcoin has pulled back to $81,300.
Down earlier in the session, front-month WTI crude oil has climbed to a one-month high of $99.40 per barrel, up 1.5% on the day, with much of the move coming in the past few minutes — though there’s no particular news that’s hit the tape.
The action may be spooking the bond market, where U.S. Treasury yields have swung from declines to gains over the past hour.
U.S. refined products (gasoline and distillates) inventories, meanwhile, continue at decade lows, according to government data.
The Nasdaq is near a session low, off 1.4% for the day.
After a volatile week of trading in stocks and bonds, Friday had gotten off to a slow start, but declines are speeding up late in the U.S. morning.
The Nasdaq is now down 1.2%, led by big drops in familiar AI-related names.
Among the Mag 7, Tesla has turned lower after opening with sizable gains following its Roadster event last night. Apple is the only gainer in the group, up 1.1%.
The selling is spreading to crypto, where bitcoin has dipped about 1% over the 30 minutes to $81,500.
Fixed income is catching a bid, with the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield now barely down for the day at 5.08% after earlier rising to 5.13%.
Bounce in neoclouds proves short-lived, with CoreWeave down 8%
After days of relentless selling, the neoclouds — former bitcoin miners turned data center providers to the fast-growing AI sector — bounced hard on Thursday, many closing the day in the green after early sharp declines.
The selling has resumed on Friday, though, with CoreWeave (CRWV) lower by 8% and extending its weekly decline to more than 20%.
Hut 8, IREN, CleanSpark, Keel Infrastructure, and Cipher Mining are all down roughly 6%.
In a note on Friday, Goldman Sachs pointed out that the widening in high-yield bond spreads is an AI story: Non-AI-related spreads were barely higher this week, while AI-related spreads widened by 25 basis points.
“We view AI-related corporate bonds, from either neoclouds or firms with significant frontier lab exposure, as being at the epicenter of the funding cost debate,” said the bank’s Amanda Lynam.
“I write to urge Anthropic to pause its planned initial public offering until the company fully and transparently addresses the artificial intelligence safety, governance, and development pace concerns it has raised,” wrote New York City Comptroller Mark Levine to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei this week.
Levine noted in the letter that as comptroller, he is an investment adviser, custodian, and trustee of NYC pension funds, with more than $325 billion in assets.
Strive raises $630 million with new preferred offering
Bitcoin treasury company Strive ASST$22.21·Market Closed upsized the offering of its new high-yielding preferred stock, SATS, to 7 million shares (from 5 million).
The sale was priced at $90 per share, giving the company gross proceeds of $630 million.
Strategy declares conditional daily dividend for STRC to begin November 1
Led by Michael Saylor, the company announced weeks ago its plan to switch to a daily dividend (from monthly) for its high-yielding preferred stock STRC.
The change is subject to a shareholder vote, which is underway, and the results will be known on Oct. 28.
Today’s announcement is thus conditional on the vote being in favor of the move to daily payments.
While strongly rebounding from its panicky lows of early summer, STRC continues to trade just below par value (yesterday’s close was $99.53), leaving Saylor and team unable to raise bitcoin-buying capital by issuing more shares.
Warsh isn't ruling out October rate hike, but markets mostly have
“I don’t prejudge meetings,” said Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, speaking at a fireside chat overnight at an IMF event. “I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings we have."
“It’s a new chapter at the Fed, and we’re not in that business anymore.”
Warsh defended the September rate hike as a necessary move to cool inflation.
He said the AI boom was the most important thing happening to global economies now, and said it was likely creating price pressures. Productivity gains will come, he said, but the road will be bumpy.
Rates are modestly higher from yesterday’s close, the 10-year U.S. yield up 2.9 basis points to 5.12%.
October Fed rate hikes odds have dipped to 15% from nearly 45% in the moments after the CPI report on Wednesday.
Crypto selloff after inflation report is temporary, Binance's Catherine Chen says
The latest inflation-driven crypto selloff is a short-term reaction rather than a sign of deeper trouble, according to Catherine Chen, Binance's head of institutional.
“The CPI-driven selloff is a sentiment shock, not a structural break,” Chen said, referring to the Consumer Price Index, a measure of U.S. inflation.
Chen expects inflation to peak around October, with clearer signs of cooling potentially emerging in March 2027. Lower energy prices and easing inflation could eventually help crypto markets recover, she said.
“A difficult trading day does not determine the outlook for the next several months,” Chen added. “The window for relief may already be approaching.”
Bitcoin climbed back above $82,000 on Friday, a day after a brief drop under $80,000, as ZEC led a broad crypto bounce with an 11% jump to about $1,230 — even as investors pulled money from the token’s only U.S. ETF.
SOL and ether each gained more than 3%, to about $106 and $2,450, and DOGE and XRP added between 2% and 3%. BNB, HYPE and TRX rose about 1%, and bitcoin was up nearly 1%, according to CoinDesk data.
The bounce hasn’t reached the ETFs. The U.S. spot ZEC fund lost about $15 million on Thursday, its fifth outflow this month, according to SoSoValue data. Ether funds shed about $60 million, and SOL funds lost nearly $10 million, their ninth straight day of withdrawals. XRP funds saw a small outflow.
Bitcoin ETFs drew a net $5 million, a thin inflow after Wednesday’s $261 million exit.
A second straight day of bitcoin ETF inflows would be the first sign the bounce from $80,000 has buyers behind it.
reference_summary: Bitcoin dipped toward $81,000 before recovering to about $81,500, down roughly 1% over 24 hours, as U.S. stocks fell sharply. The Nasdaq dropped 2.15% and an index measuring expected stock-market turbulence jumped 22%. Oil also rose above $101 a barrel amid reports of an attack on a Saudi pipeline.

title: MSCI approves rules that could eject Strategy, Metaplanet from equity indexes
article_text:
MSCI approves rules that could eject Strategy, Metaplanet from equity indexes. MSCI approves rules that could eject Strategy, Metaplanet from equity indexes
The rules proposed in August would see companies that exist mainly to hold investments as no longer eligible for index inclusion.
- MSCI finalized rules that could remove Strategy, Metaplanet and other investment-heavy companies from its global equity indexes after trading closes on Nov. 30.
- The affected firms will be named on Nov. 11.
- JPMorgan analysts have estimated that Strategy’s exclusion could prompt about $2.8 billion in stock outflows, though index funds’ forced sales would affect the company’s shares, not its bitcoin holdings.
MSCI, one of the world's biggest stock index providers, finalized rules proposed in August that could remove shares of leading bitcoin 
Under the rules announced Thursday, companies that mostly hold investments rather than running a real business will be deemed ineligible for MSCI's Global Investable Market Indexes. The final list of affected firms is due Nov. 11 and the change takes effect at the close of Nov. 30.
The decision is important because it affects demand for the companies’ shares. Many investors gain exposure to stock markets by placing their money in funds that track an index. When a company is added to the index, those funds must buy its stock. When it is removed, they must sell, whatever the fund managers think of the company.
"The MSCI episode highlights a growing tension between traditional index construction and the rise of companies that treat Bitcoin as a core treasury asset rather than a secondary holding,” decentralized infrastructure network ZEROBASE said on X. “Passive capital has become an important source of demand for these stocks; any sustained reduction in that bid could tighten the equity-issuance window that several of them rely on to fund further purchases."
The risk is biggest for Tysons Corner, Virginia-based Strategy, the largest publicly listed bitcoin holder, with 848,250 BTC worth about $69.67 billion, according to Bitcoin Treasuries. It tends to fund its purchases by selling preferred shares such as STRC and STRK.
JPMorgan analysts have estimated that index exclusion could trigger outflows of about $2.8 billion from MSTR stock. The shares closed at $151.29 on Thursday, down about 72% from their record high of $543 in November 2024. Tokyo-based Metplanet, which closed at 277 yen ($1.75) on Friday, peaked at 1,930 yen in June 2025, according to TradingView.
Any selling would hit the shares, not bitcoin. The funds would be dumping the stock, which does not necessarily mean Strategy would sell its bitcoin.
But weaker demand for the shares could make it harder for these companies to raise the money they use to buy more bitcoin, a strategy they have long pursued to stack up more coins.
Strategy's founder, Michael Saylor, has described the company as an operating business with a software arm, and its bitcoin treasury as a distinct business segment. He has rejected comparisons with investment funds. Strategy, originally MicroStrategy, sells business intelligence software to companies including Coca-Cola and Porsche.
How MSCI decides who is out
MSCI already excludes investment funds and similar vehicles. The new rules extend that to companies that look like them.
First, MSCI checks whether a company has substantial operating assets, meaning assets tied to a real business. If it fails, the company faces a second test based on five financial ratios covering expenses, cash flow, changes in asset values and reliance on outside financing. A company flagged on four or more of the five is ineligible.
To avoid constant churn in the index, MSCI has added buffers. A member is removed only if it fails the screen in each of its two most recent annual filing periods. A company outside the index is blocked from joining if it fails in either of its two most recent periods.
In a first test run using May 2026 data, MSCI flagged three companies for possible removal from its ACWI Investable Market Index. They were Strategy, Metaplanet and Yellow Cake, a U.K. uranium investment company.
MSCI is also ending the temporary measures it announced in October 2025 for companies with digital assets making up 50% or more of total assets. Those measures froze increases in the share counts used in the index and put off additions and size-segment moves for those companies. From the November review, they will be judged under the new rules instead.
reference_summary: MSCI finalized rules that could remove Strategy, Metaplanet and other companies focused mainly on holding investments from its stock indexes, the lists of companies that many investment funds follow. Affected companies will be named on November 11, with changes taking effect after trading on November 30. Funds following those indexes would have to sell the companies' shares, but that would not automatically require Strategy to sell its bitcoin.

title: XRP has failed to make holders rich like bitcoin and ether. Here’s why
article_text:
XRP has failed to make holders rich like bitcoin and ether. Here’s why. XRP has failed to make holders rich like bitcoin and ether. Here’s why
XRP remains below its 2017-cycle high while bitcoin, ether and other major tokens have surged, enriching their holders.
- XRP trades around $1.33, about 62.5% below its January 2018 peak, while Bitcoin, Ether and several other major cryptocurrencies have surpassed their previous highs.
- Analysts attribute XRP’s lagging price partly to a sharp increase in circulating supply, weak fund inflows and declining trading activity and network use.
- Ripple’s focus on payments, XRP’s limited exposure to popular crypto sectors and years of regulatory uncertainty from the S.E.C. case have also weighed on demand.
Holding is widely touted as a great way to build wealth in the crypto market, but it hasn't worked for every coin.
Take XRP (XRP), the payments-focused cryptocurrency native to the XRP Ledger and the world’s fifth-largest digital asset by market value.
The token is still trading well below its 2017 cycle high, while most other major cryptocurrencies have climbed far above theirs. In 2017, crypto broke into the mainstream, pulling in new users and investors during the frenzied run that carried into the first week or two of 2018.
XRP currently trades around $1.33, down 62.5% from its early January 2018 peak of $3.55. In other words, an XRP buyer from that peak is still underwater nearly nine years later. (XRP did briefly top its old high, reaching $3.66 in July 2025 before crashing.)
Bitcoin 
Bitcoin, ether and many other tokens have pulled back sharply from their 2025 peaks, yet remain far above their 2017 highs.
Too many coins
Analysts point first to XRP’s supply.
"Circulating supply grew 63%, from 38.7B in 2017 to 63.1B, while XRP's total market value fell only about 3%," Nicolai Sondergaard, senior research analyst at analytics firm Nansen, told CoinDesk. "More XRP in circulation means each token represents a smaller share of roughly the same total value."
Circulating supply is the number of coins on the market, and as it grows, each coin represents a smaller share of the total.
Oliver Carding, head of marketing at Tesseract Group, says XRP looks better when measured by total value instead of price.
"On value, XRP recovered," he said. "About 63% more XRP is in circulation than at that peak, so the same circulating market capitalization would mean a price roughly 39% lower."
Tesseract is an institutional digital asset management firm that manages over $500 million in assets under management.
Weaker demand
U.S.-listed exchange-traded funds, or ETFs, have opened the door for institutional investors to take exposure to digital assets. While bitcoin and ether funds have pulled in billions, XRP funds have lagged big time.
"ETF uptake has also been muted relative to $BTC and $ETH," said Paul Howard, senior director at market-making firm Wincent.
To date, XRP funds have pulled in just $1.80 billion in investor money since debuting nearly a year ago, according to data source SoSoValue. Bitcoin ETFs often attract over $1 billion in investor money in a single day.
Nansen's data also shows trading activity has weakened, with XRP spot volume down 53.5%, perpetual futures volume down 44%, and active addresses down 10.7%.
Ripple's focus
Ripple, the payments company closely tied to XRP, has focused on cross-border payments rather than chasing sectors such as DeFi, AI, and memecoins, which have attracted greater capital flows and deeper integration with traditional finance.
"Ripple, meanwhile, has been working hard to build payment infrastructure, RLUSD and trade financing products around the usage of the ledger and coin, and this has taken focus from just core XRP," Howard said.
Investors also have more choices now.
"The role of DeFi for investment into ETH, SOL and HYPE has also been a new narrative which $XRP has not focused on," Howard said.
The SEC case
Ripple’s legal fight with U.S. regulators also held XRP back.
The Securities and Exchange Commission sued Ripple and two of its executives in December 2020, saying the company had raised about $1.3 billion by selling XRP without registering it as a security.
A federal judge ruled in 2023 that XRP sales on public exchanges were not securities offerings, but that sales to institutional investors were. In 2024, Ripple was ordered to pay a $125 million penalty. The case ended in August 2025, when both sides dropped their appeals.
Carding said the prolonged regulatory uncertainty helps explain why the token missed its old high during the 2021 crypto bull run, when Coinbase suspended trading.
“The SEC case helps explain why XRP did not revisit its 2018 high in 2021, when Coinbase suspended trading, but the appeals were dropped in August 2025 with XRP above $3,” Carding said. “Since then, XRP is down about 59%, against 32% for bitcoin and 44% for ether, and its circulating market capitalisation is down about 56%.”
Not the only laggard
XRP isn't the only coin trading below its early 2018 highs.
"On price, six of the other nine assets in the January 2018 top ten are further below their levels of that week," Carding said.
For those watching XRP, Carding has a suggestion.
"What I would watch is XRP against bitcoin, alongside net monthly distribution after re-escrow and changes in fund holdings," he said. "Relative weakness that persists as distribution slows would point to weaker demand."
In plain English, Carding is watching whether XRP underperforms bitcoin even as fewer new XRP tokens enter the market through Ripple’s escrow releases. If supply growth slows but XRP still lags bitcoin, it would suggest that investor demand for XRP is weakening.
reference_summary: XRP trades around $1.33, about 62.5% below its January 2018 peak, although it briefly exceeded that peak in July 2025. Analysts link its weak price performance to a roughly 63% increase in coins available on the market, weaker investor demand and trading activity, and years of uncertainty during Ripple's dispute with U.S. regulators.

title: An OpenAI agent ran out of Ethereum funds, and took from a wallet it did not own
article_text:
An OpenAI agent ran out of Ethereum funds, and took from a wallet it did not own. An OpenAI agent ran out of Ethereum funds, and took from a wallet it did not own
The research model derived funded Sepolia addresses from public seed phrases, questioned whether using the money was ethical, then called the funds “effectively abandoned” and used them anyway.
- An internal OpenAI research model used a publicly available recovery phrase to access and spend from another person’s cryptocurrency wallet after it ran out of funds during a coding assignment.
- The June 26 incident occurred on Ethereum’s Sepolia test network, whose tokens have no connection to ether traded on the main network, and OpenAI discovered it on Sept. 25.
- The model completed the assignment without disclosing the source of the funds, prompting OpenAI to add internet-access restrictions and increased monitoring.
An OpenAI research model stuck without funds on an Ethereum test network went looking for someone else’s wallet, found one through recovery phrases that were already public, and spent from it to finish a coding assignment, the company disclosed Thursday.
The incident occurred on June 26 during training of an internal model in the GPT-5.6 Sol family, and OpenAI discovered it on Sept. 25, according to its incident report.
The model needed no hacking skills to get in.
A recovery phrase, also called a seed phrase, is a list of words that generates a wallet’s secret keys; whoever has those words can recreate the accounts and spend from them without ever touching the owner’s device.
The assignment let the model deploy contracts, programs that run on a blockchain, but gave it no funded wallet to pay the fees. After its attempts to get free test tokens failed, it wrote a script that checked 362 addresses generated from recovery phrases commonly used by developers and found one with enough money.
“But using public known key/funds ethically?” the model asked itself in its recorded reasoning, before deciding that a public phrase and test tokens made it acceptable.
The spending happened on Sepolia, a separate network where developers rehearse Ethereum applications before launching them. Its tokens only pay for testing and aren't linked to the ether traded on Ethereum’s main network.
The deployment went through, and the wallet paid the fees. When the model reported back, it said the work was done and left out where the money came from. OpenAI said it has since added restrictions on internet access and more monitoring.
Crypto and AI companies are building agents that hold wallets and pay for services without a person signing off on each step.
OpenAI’s model ran out of money mid-task, found a wallet that wasn’t its own and spent from it without asking. Had it been on Ethereum’s main network, that would have been real ether taken from someone else’s account.
reference_summary: OpenAI disclosed that an internal research model used publicly available recovery words to access someone else's cryptocurrency wallet and pay fees after running out of funds during a coding task. The spending occurred on Ethereum's Sepolia testing network, whose tokens are separate from ether traded on the main network. OpenAI said the model did not disclose where the funds came from, and the company added internet-access restrictions and increased monitoring.

title: Bitcoin buyers snap up a brief drop below $80,000 as Asian stocks rebound
article_text:
Bitcoin buyers snap up a brief drop below $80,000 as Asian stocks rebound. Bitcoin buyers snap up a brief drop below $80,000 as Asian stocks rebound
Bitcoin tore back to $82,500 within two hours of dipping under $80,000, and chipmakers in Seoul recovered from their worst close since April.
- Bitcoin rebounded 1.3% to nearly $82,000 after briefly falling below $80,000, while ZEC led major cryptocurrencies with an 8% gain.
- Asian stocks also recovered, led by gains in South Korean chipmakers, though Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing slipped amid concerns about artificial intelligence spending.
- Traders are watching whether Bitcoin can break above $84,000 and awaiting remarks from Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh after hotter-than-expected inflation data.
Bitcoin rose 1.3% to nearly $82,000 as of Friday Asian morning hours after buyers pounced on a brief drop below $80,000, with Asian chip stocks bouncing back from Thursday’s rout.
ZEC was the standout among the majors, jumping 8% to about $1,190. SOL, ether, XRP and TRX added about 1% apiece, and BNB went nowhere, according to CoinDesk data.
Bitcoin’s break below $80,000 lasted all of two hours. The slide on Thursday took it to about $79,800, cutting through the roughly $80,400 low that buyers had defended twice in the past week, and that’s where they showed up again. Bitcoin was back near $82,500 within two hours and held above $81,000 through Asian trading.
Stock traders bought the dip too. MSCI’s Asia Pacific equities gauge climbed 1.3%, with roughly three shares rising for every one that fell. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix both gained more than 2%, and South Korea’s Kospi jumped nearly 3% after closing at its lowest since April on Thursday.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing was the odd one out, slipping even after an upbeat outlook as worries over AI spending hung around.
Bonds handed back some of Thursday’s rush into safety. Treasuries fell across the curve, pushing the 10-year yield up a basis point to 5.07%. Traders now turn to Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, who speaks at the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok on Friday, two days after September inflation came in hotter than expected.
A push back above $84,000, where Wednesday’s post-inflation spike ran out of steam, would show this bounce has real buyers behind it.
reference_summary: Bitcoin briefly fell to about $79,800 before buyers pushed it back near $82,500 within two hours, and it traded near $82,000 during Friday morning in Asia. Asian stocks also recovered, led by South Korean chipmakers, while ZEC rose 8% to about $1,190. Traders were awaiting remarks from U.S. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh after inflation came in higher than expected.

title: At the White House, crypto policy vacancy looms large
article_text:
At the White House, crypto policy vacancy looms large. At the White House, crypto policy vacancy looms large
The departure of President Donald Trump's crypto adviser, Patrick Witt, leaves the digital assets office vacant and its policy aims uncertain.
- The exit of President Donald Trump’s crypto adviser, Patrick Witt, wasn’t a surprise, but it leaves the White House without an explicit digital assets policy presence.
- The White House insists that crypto is still a priority, but its recent naming of a new AI czar left crypto off the role despite its previous inclusion.
When President Donald Trump returned to the White House last year, he not only shed his earlier resistance to crypto technology but embraced the industry with the hiring of a high-profile crypto czar and the establishment of his President’s Council of Advisors for Digital Assets.
Almost two years later, that policy push seems to have gone quiet for the moment, with the departure of Patrick Witt, who had been the final crypto adviser running that office. And when the president recently ushered in a new artificial intelligence czar, the job that was once split between crypto and AI seemed to have dropped its crypto remit.
So who is minding the store for crypto policy at the White House? It's not clear, even as a handful of people on Capitol Hill continue to suggest that the final weeks of the congressional session after the November elections could still see some legislative action for the industry. The White House still has a staff of policy advisers, and Trump's administration now boasts several crypto regulatory irons in the fire at agencies such as the Securities and Exchange Commission. But no new name has been explicitly attached to Trump's in-house crypto initiatives.
A White House official told CoinDesk on Thursday that Witt's work was appreciated and wished him "the best of luck in the future endeavors." The official didn’t comment on who would be taking over.
"Crypto and Clarity Act will continue to be a priority for the president," the official said.
The White House's digital assets policy work was never a large operation, but the advisers were highly vocal at times, and their presence could put an important administrative stamp on crypto goals. The effort began several weeks before Trump returned to office in 2025, when the president-elect named David Sacks, the former PayPal executive, as his incoming AI and crypto czar.
Trump also tapped a little-known former college football player, Bo Hines, to be the first director of the digital assets advisory council — at first a one-person effort, but eventually adding a deputy. Hines quickly became the crypto face of the White House, taking constant meetings with crypto insiders and appearing on event stages. And his brief tenure of about eight months concluded with a major win for the industry in Congress: the passage of the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act into law.
A White House signing and celebration ensued, in which many of the most prominent names in crypto enjoyed front-row seats. Less than two weeks later, the administration released a comprehensive crypto agenda that set out its specific plans for fostering the sector in the U.S.
Having helped establish the U.S. law for stablecoin issuers, Hines took a job running the U.S. arm of the leading issuer, Tether. Meanwhile, a consulting firm he set up with his father and another partner, Nxum, was also paid millions of dollars as the main provider of services for a new political action committee, first revealed in reporting by CoinDesk. The super PAC was funded mostly by Tether's U.S. financial partner, Cantor Fitzgerald, and led by a Tether exec.
This week, the Wall Street Journal reported that Hines' Nxum, had received payments from Tether for consulting services while Hines was at the White House working on the GENIUS Act.
Hines' deputy on the council, Witt, took over for Hines as its new executive director. Another former football star, Witt also had a greater depth of Washington experience, and he became the face of the White House's push for the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act. Over the ensuing months of negotiations, Witt didn't conceal his frustration, regularly taking to social media site X to fume about those he saw as getting in the way of the Senate bill that would erect a U.S. regulatory scaffold for crypto markets.
During that legislative process, Sacks stepped down from the czar role in March, leaving Witt and his deputy, Harry Jung, trying to manage the administration's crypto stance. That was complicated by the fact that President Trump's own crypto empire figured prominently in the talks, as Democrats demanded that senior government officials be blocked from personal crypto ties.
As the negotiations dragged further into the year — and closer to the elections — the White House offered some concessions that would have applied unprecedented ethics constraints on the president's digital assets involvement, though Democrats concluded that the agreement didn't go far enough.
Witt had confirmed in July that he had military-service commitments on the horizon with the Georgia National Guard, but he stayed to complete Clarity Act negotiations, even as his deputy left to join Hines’ Nxum. The legislation slammed into a political roadblock a month ago, failing to advance in a Senate floor vote before the chamber dispersed for a lengthy break leading up to next month's elections.
Following rumors this week that Witt had already exited, he posted Wednesday night at around midnight to confirm his departure. He thanked agency chiefs and lawmakers that had helped with Clarity, saying that "with regulators and elected officials like you, I rest easy knowing the future of digital asset innovation in America is bright." He said he'd be moving into the private sector.
Crypto insiders say they aren't sure who they'll be dealing with as their market-structure hopes have largely fizzled for the moment.
When Trump moved earlier this month to re-establish an AI overseer, hiring former SEC Chairman and current intelligence director Jay Clayton to lead his Super Intelligence Force, the job no longer mentions a crypto element. While AI and crypto enjoy some overlapping territory, Clayton comes with a rocky crypto history, having been the SEC chief that first began its stance that would be labeled "regulation by enforcement."
reference_summary: Patrick Witt's departure leaves the White House without a named adviser leading President Donald Trump's cryptocurrency policy office. A White House official said cryptocurrency and the Clarity Act, proposed rules for cryptocurrency markets, remain priorities, but did not identify a replacement. The vacancy follows the bill's failure to advance in a Senate vote before the election break.

title: Banks could slow stablecoin growth by paying savers more, BIS paper finds
article_text:
Banks could slow stablecoin growth by paying savers more, BIS paper finds. Banks could slow stablecoin growth by paying savers more, BIS paper finds
A BIS working paper found a 1 basis point rise in U.S. bank deposit rates predicted slower stablecoin growth, cutting ten-week growth from 15% to 12%.
- A BIS working paper found a 1 basis point rise in U.S. bank deposit rates predicted slower stablecoin growth, cutting ten-week growth from 15% to 12%.
- The effect was stronger for Circle's USDC than Tether's USDT, which the authors linked to USDC's closer ties to U.S. users.
- The authors say banks retain some influence over stablecoin adoption through deposit pricing, though the sample covers only one high-rate period.
Banks may be able to slow the growth of stablecoins like USDT and USDC by paying savers more, according to a working paper published by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS).
Researchers Rashad Ahmed and Iñaki Aldasoro studied weekly data from January 2019 to June 2025, accounting for bitcoin prices, Treasury yields and broader financial conditions. They found that a one-week, one basis point rise in average bank deposit rates predicted slower stablecoin growth.
That small figure, just 0.01 percentage points, cut average ten-week growth in stablecoin market capitalization from about 15% to about 12%, the paper found.
Under the authors’ preferred estimate, which adjusts for banks raising rates in response to stablecoin growth, the effect was roughly three times larger, slowing growth to about 6%, though the authors flagged some weakness in that method. In both cases, growth slowed but did not reverse.
The relationship was stronger for Circle’s USDC than Tether’s USDT, a pattern the authors said was consistent with USDC’s closer ties to U.S. users.
The findings add evidence to a debate that has drawn warnings from bank executives. Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan warned in January that as much as $6 trillion in deposits could move into stablecoins and related products offering returns, potentially reducing lending capacity and raising borrowing costs.
The effect is partly based on where issuers put their reserves. A December Federal Reserve staff analysis explained that money placed in stablecoins can return to banks as issuer deposits, changing who supplies banks’ funding even when total deposits remain unchanged.
Larger, uninsured balances could require banks to keep more liquid assets and leave less room for long-term loans that financial institutions issue.
Paying more to retain customers also raises banks’ funding costs. The Fed analysis suggested banks could target better rates at customers most likely to switch, while keeping lower rates for less mobile depositors.
The BIS paper does not establish losses of bank deposits or lending. Its sample covers one high-rate episode, and the findings may change as yield-bearing stablecoins and tokenized money market funds gain ground.
Banks “retain some influence over the pace of that adoption through deposit pricing,” the authors wrote.
reference_summary: A Bank for International Settlements working paper found that higher interest payments on U.S. bank savings were linked to slower growth in the total value of stablecoins, digital currencies designed to maintain a steady value. A 0.01 percentage-point rise in deposit rates predicted average growth over ten weeks slowing from about 15% to 12%, with a stronger relationship for Circle's USDC than Tether's USDT. The study covered only one period of high interest rates and did not establish that banks lost deposits or reduced lending.

title: Chip-stock bets lost $52 million in 10 minutes with Wall Street shut
article_text:
Chip-stock bets lost $52 million in 10 minutes with Wall Street shut. Chip-stock bets lost $52 million in 10 minutes with Wall Street shut
A 10-minute flush hit round-the-clock chip-stock contracts while U.S. markets were shut, leaving traders with no real share price to lean on.
- Nearly $52 million in leveraged bets tied to chip stocks and semiconductor funds were liquidated in 10 minutes Saturday, even as Wall Street was closed.
- The sell-off began on Binance and spread within seconds to Hyperliquid, with traders betting on higher prices accounting for about $38 million of the liquidations.
- Because the contracts trade around the clock, weekend prices were driven by crypto traders rather than actual share prices, which will provide a benchmark when U.S. markets reopen Monday.
A sudden wave of selling wiped out nearly $52 million in crypto traders’ leveraged bets on chip stocks in 10 minutes on Saturday, while the shares themselves sat idle with Wall Street closed for the weekend.
Those bets were placed through perpetual futures, contracts that track a stock’s price and trade around the clock on crypto exchanges, so traders can buy and sell chip stocks on a Saturday night.
A trader who borrows to make a bigger bet gets closed out automatically when losses eat through their deposit, and the forced selling can push prices lower for the next trader in line.
About $51.6 million in positions tied to chip stocks and semiconductor funds were force-closed between 21:22 and 21:32 UTC, according to CoinGlass data, and about $38 million of that came from traders betting on higher prices.
SOXL, a fund that triples the daily moves in chip shares, took the biggest hit at about $12.7 million. SanDisk and SK Hynix contracts followed at about $10.8 million each.
The selling started on Binance, according to a review of the trades by David Jeong, chief executive of trading firm Tread.fi, who placed the first large SanDisk and Micron sell orders on Binance at 21:21:59 UTC.
Less than a second later, orders hit Hyperliquid, a crypto exchange where Trade XYZ lists stock-tracking contracts, and roughly 10 addresses opened bets against six chip-linked contracts within 1.8 seconds.
Binance handled about $21.9 million of SanDisk trading in that first minute, against $3.1 million on Trade XYZ.
Memory-chip shares were already coming off a rough week as investors weighed new competition from Chinese chipmaker CXMT.
With the stock market shut, there was no real share price for these contracts to follow, so traders were reacting only to each other. Trade XYZ’s rules let trading on the platform set its own reference prices until outside stock quotes come back.
Those quotes return when U.S. markets open Monday, which will show how far Saturday’s prices strayed from where the shares actually trade.
reference_summary: Nearly $52 million in bets tied to chip stocks were automatically closed in ten minutes on Saturday after losses exhausted traders' deposits. The selling began on Binance and quickly spread to Hyperliquid, mainly hitting people betting on higher prices with borrowed money. These contracts trade around the clock, so their prices moved while the actual U.S. stock market was closed.

title: Stablecoin supply stalls, but payments jump 45% as Visa, Mastercard and Stripe connect crypto to cash
article_text:
Stablecoin supply stalls, but payments jump 45% as Visa, Mastercard and Stripe connect crypto to cash. Stablecoin supply stalls, but payments jump 45% as Visa, Mastercard and Stripe connect crypto to cash
Analytics firm Allium said stablecoin payments hit $482 billion this year so far, up 45%, as card spending surges and global payment firms add crypto rails.
- Stablecoin payments grew 45% to $482 billion this year through September, despite circulating supply stalling in 2026, according to a fresh report by blockchain analytics firm Allium.
- Mastercard, Stripe and Visa all announced services this week that combine stablecoins with familiar payment systems as digital dollars become increasingly part of global money movement.
- Businesses want stablecoins being integrated into their existing financial operations, instead of running separate systems for digital assets, said CEO of Paris-based enterprise payments firm Fipto.
Stablecoin supply has barely budged this year, but the digital dollars already in circulation are doing more work in payments, according to a fresh report from blockchain analytics firm Allium.
Stablecoin payments are growing at a rapid pace, reaching $482 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 45% from a year earlier, the report found.
That growth contrasts with the broader stablecoin market. The total value of stablecoins — cryptocurrencies tied to fiat currencies such as the U.S. dollar — in circulation stood at about $305 billion at the end of September, up a meager 0.4% since the start of the year, according to the report.
The number of payments grew even more, jumping 71% to over 1 billion, the report said, suggesting that stablecoins are changing hands more often without much new supply entering the market.
Stablecoin-linked cards showed some of the fastest growth. Spending measured by Allium reached $3.9 billion through September, ten times the amount a year earlier. Small purchases — under $50 — accounted for 84% of the increase in card transactions.
Stablecoins meet traditional payment rails
Three announcements earlier this week offered a glimpse of how stablecoins are becoming increasingly part of global payments.
Mastercard (MA) introduced Thursday its Global Money Platform with BVNK, the stablecoin infrastructure firm it acquired in August. The service combines traditional currency accounts, stablecoin balances, conversions, card spending and bank payouts through one connection.
Banks and fintechs can use the platform to offer accounts that hold both fiat currencies and stablecoins, the firm said. Payments firms Nuvei and Marqeta are among the first customers integrating that service.
Stripe, meanwhile, is working with Plasma 
The companies said they plan to let customers spend from the balance that matches their purchase, cutting unnecessary currency conversions. Stripe's expanded card infrastructure covers more than 30 countries, with plans to reach over 100 by next year.
Read more: Stripe to expand stablecoin cards to over 100 countries by the end of the year
And Visa (V) said it is bringing stablecoins into the funding side of international payments.
The company said Inyo Global, a payment orchestration firm for fintech, money transmitter, banks, became the first provider to put Visa Direct's stablecoin prefunding service into commercial use. Payment firms can use Circle's (CRCL) dollar stablecoin USDC 
A small slice of a vast payments market
That rapid growth of stablecoin payments comes with some caveats. Of $97.9 trillion in raw stablecoin transfers through September, Allium classified just $2.4 trillion, or 2.5%, as end-user activity after filtering out exchange, decentralized finance and automated transactions. Its $482 billion payments estimate comes from that smaller pool, the report said.
Stablecoin cards also remain a tiny fraction of conventional payments. Allium estimated that second-quarter spending through those cards amounted to just 0.03% of Visa's $4 trillion in payment volume.
For payment companies, that leaves a large market to pursue. Nuvei CEO Phil Fayer, whose company is among the first to integrate Mastercard's new platform, said stablecoins are becoming part of how businesses move money across borders and currencies.
"The future of global commerce depends on money moving as freely as the businesses and consumers it serves, across borders, currencies and increasingly, between traditional and digital forms of money," Fayer said.
The recent efforts by Mastercard, Stripe and Visa to incorporate stablecoins on blockchain rails reinforce that trend. Companies increasingly want stablecoins integrated into their existing financial operations, instead of running separate systems for digital assets, according to Patrick Mollard, co-founder and CEO of Paris-based Fipto, a stablecoin-powered business payments firm.
“The distinction between 'traditional' and 'digital' money is less important than giving businesses the ability to use whichever rail makes most sense for a particular payment or treasury operation,” he said in a note shared with CoinDesk.
“Businesses don't want separate crypto infrastructure sitting alongside their existing financial operations,” Mollard said. “They want to move between fiat and stablecoins within the same payments and treasury environment.”
reference_summary: Payments using stablecoins, digital currencies designed to track currencies such as the U.S. dollar, reached $482 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 45% from a year earlier, according to Allium. The total value of stablecoins in circulation rose only 0.4% over the same period. Mastercard, Stripe and Visa announced services connecting stablecoins with existing accounts, cards and international payments.

title: Bitcoin’s $100,000 year-end hope divides analysts as inflation clouds outlook
article_text:
Bitcoin’s $100,000 year-end hope divides analysts as inflation clouds outlook. Bitcoin’s $100,000 year-end hope divides analysts as inflation clouds outlook
Bitwise sees a potential return above $100,000, while LO:TECH expects a narrower trading range as interest-rate uncertainty weighs on the market.
- Bitwise sees bitcoin potentially topping $100,000 by year-end, supported by institutional adoption and demand for hard assets.
- LO:TECH expects an $85,000–$95,000 year-end range as inflation and rate-hike risks constrain gains.
- Laser Digital sees potential for a short squeeze, while CoinShares says a sustained breakout needs renewed buying.
Bitcoin 
The forecasts highlight a divide over timing. Analysts see longer-term support from institutional investment, regulatory progress and concerns about government debt, but disagree on whether those forces can drive a breakout before the end of 2026.
Ryan Rasmussen, head of research at Bitwise, expects bitcoin to emerge from the coming weeks’ uncertainty at a higher valuation.
“We believe bitcoin ends the year higher, potentially above $100,000,” Rasmussen told CoinDesk.
He identified three longer-term drivers: institutional buying through exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and corporate purchases; demand for hard assets amid inflation, rising debt and currency debasement; and clearer regulation that reduces the perceived risk of owning crypto.
“In our view, these tailwinds significantly outweigh the potential headwinds,” he said.
The macro hurdle
Rasmussen nevertheless expects volatility around a possible late-October Federal Reserve rate increase and November’s U.S. midterm elections. A breakout would be difficult in that environment, he said, although the uncertainty could create an opportunity for investors to build positions.
Adam Morgan McCarthy, head of research at LO:TECH, a London-based crypto trading and market data firm, is more cautious. His base case is an $85,000–$95,000 trading range into year-end.
“Macro has gone against Bitcoin all year, with the Fed hiking in September and a December hike priced at roughly 75%,” McCarthy said. “This will continue to weigh on bitcoin.”
The Fed raised its benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point in September. Inflation figures released Oct. 14 complicated the outlook: consumer prices rose 0.6% from the previous month, while core prices increased 0.3%. Gasoline accounted for more than half of the headline increase.
McCarthy said a return above $100,000 would require expectations for a December hike to give way to a pause, supported by easing oil prices and inflation.
James Butterfill, head of research at CoinShares, sees a similar tension between persistent inflation and weakening employment. Cooling prices would give the Fed more room to respond to labor-market weakness; further inflation pressure could keep policy restrictive and weigh on bitcoin.
The world’s largest cryptocurrency was trading around $81,500 at publication time.
Less leverage, potential for a squeeze
Luca Invernizzi, senior derivatives trader at Laser Digital, Nomura’s crypto subsidiary, expects bitcoin to remain largely a macro trade into year-end, taking its direction from longer-dated Treasury yields.
He described the rebound from summer lows as unconvincing, citing thin volumes, fading ETF inflows and slowing corporate buying.
Positioning offers more encouragement. Leverage has largely been flushed out of bitcoin, with much of the speculative excess moving into altcoins, Invernizzi said.
McCarthy also sees fewer crowded bullish positions that could unravel. Funding rates, payments between perpetual futures traders, are at or below zero, while August’s rally was driven by traders closing bearish bets rather than adding new bullish positions.
That reduces the fuel for forced selling and leaves room for another squeeze higher.
“A clean break above $90K for BTC could trigger another round of short covering,” Invernizzi said.
With implied volatility back near its lows and options pricing still tilted toward downside protection, he sees upside calls as an attractive way to position for a rally without chasing bitcoin in the spot market.
Longer-term demand
The broader industry’s recovery provides another source of optimism.
In a research note to clients earlier this week authored by Peter Christiansen, Citi (C) said total crypto market capitalization rose from roughly $2.1 trillion to nearly $3 trillion during the third quarter. Institutional ETF flows turned positive, while activity across exchanges, stablecoins and digital asset infrastructure improved.
The bank also sees investors increasingly looking beyond crypto prices toward businesses supporting tokenization, custody, stablecoins and settlement. Regulatory progress continues despite the Clarity Act’s failure to advance, Citi said.
Butterfill cautioned that investment-product flows have since slowed following $11.1 billion of inflows since mid-July. He views that as uncertainty rather than deteriorating bitcoin fundamentals, but said sustained gains require renewed buying.
Like Rasmussen, he sees concerns about government finances as a potential longer-term source of demand. Higher Treasury yields typically hurt bitcoin by tightening financial conditions, but that relationship could shift if investors increasingly interpret those yields as compensation for fiscal risk.
“Our bias is towards higher prices over the medium term, but we would want to see the fiscal argument translate into sustained allocations before expecting a decisive breakout,” Butterfill said.
Rasmussen is more confident those forces will translate into gains sooner.
“Once the market churns through this period, we expect bitcoin to rerate significantly higher,” he said.
Read more: The Clarity Act stalled. Bankers aren’t hitting the brakes yet on crypto dealmaking
reference_summary: Analysts disagree over whether bitcoin, trading near $81,500, can exceed $100,000 by the end of 2026. Bitwise's Ryan Rasmussen sees that as possible because of demand from large investors and clearer rules, while LO:TECH's Adam Morgan McCarthy expects $85,000–$95,000 as inflation and possible interest-rate increases limit gains. CoinShares' James Butterfill said a sustained rise would require renewed buying.

title: Deutsche Bank targets Asia crypto custody expansion in 2027 as German launch nears
article_text:
Deutsche Bank targets Asia crypto custody expansion in 2027 as German launch nears. Deutsche Bank targets Asia crypto custody expansion in 2027 as German launch nears
The service will initially support bitcoin, ether and the stablecoins USDC, EURC and EURAU, with the bank managing clients’ wallets and private keys.
- Deutsche Bank plans to bring its crypto custody service to Asia in 2027 and launch it in Germany within weeks, its corporate bank co-head told Reuters.
- The service will initially support bitcoin, ether and the stablecoins USDC, EURC and EURAU, with the bank managing clients’ wallets and private keys.
- The bank also plans stablecoin conversion, tokenized deposits and digital bond issuance as part of a target of roughly 8% annual revenue growth by 2028.
Deutsche Bank (DB) plans to bring its crypto custody service to Asia in 2027, extending its push into digital assets as it prepares to launch the service in Germany within weeks.
The German banking giant, Reuters reported citing the firm’s co-head, also plans to offer stablecoin conversion, tokenized deposits and services that help clients issue digital bonds and other blockchain-based securities.
The move could give institutional clients in Asia access to crypto services through an established global bank, without having to manage their own crypto wallets or private keys. It’s unclear which Asian financial services it will target first.
Deutsche Bank's custody service will allow corporate and institutional clients to hold and transfer cryptocurrencies, with the bank handling the technology needed to keep the assets secure.
The bank said in September that its initial offering would support bitcoin, ether and stablecoins including USDC, EURC and EURAU. The German launch remains subject to regulatory approval.
The bank received authorization from Germany’s financial regulator, BaFin, under the EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) rules on October 12, according to the European Securities and Markets Authority’s interim register.
Podobnik said the expansion is part of Deutsche Bank’s broader plan to achieve roughly 8% compound annual revenue growth in its corporate bank from 2025 to 2028.
The Asia rollout would extend the custody service beyond Europe as banks seek a larger role in managing digital assets for institutional clients. Deutsche Bank has worked with Bitpanda and Taurus on its custody plans, and joins rivals such as Standard Chartered and BBVA in offering crypto custody.
reference_summary: Deutsche Bank plans to launch a service for holding and safeguarding clients' cryptocurrency in Germany within weeks and expand it to Asia in 2027, Reuters reported, citing a senior bank executive. The bank would manage the wallets and secret access keys, initially supporting bitcoin, ether, USDC, EURC and EURAU. The German launch remains subject to regulatory approval, and the first Asian markets have not been identified.

title: Bitcoin, Korea’s Kospi and Nasdaq futures rally as China GDP beats estimates
article_text:
Bitcoin, Korea’s Kospi and Nasdaq futures rally as China GDP beats estimates. Bitcoin, Korea’s Kospi and Nasdaq futures rally as China GDP beats estimates
Bitcoin, Nasdaq futures and Asian stocks rally as stronger-than-expected China GDP and falling oil prices lift risk appetite.
- Global markets rallied Monday as stronger Chinese economic data and lower oil prices revived investors’ appetite for risk.
- Bitcoin traded near $82,500, while Nasdaq futures gained more than 1% and major Asian stock indexes advanced after last week’s technology-led losses.
- China’s economy grew 4.5% from a year earlier in the third quarter, while retail sales exceeded expectations and signaled stronger domestic demand.
Financial markets are a sea of green on Monday as upbeat China data and lower oil prices revive investor risk appetite.
Starting with bitcoin. The leading cryptocurrency by market value was trading around $83,000 during early European hours, up 1% since midnight UTC and 1.60% over the past 24 hours. Nasdaq futures rose more than 1%, alongside a 1.8% gain in Japan’s Nikkei and a 0.6% advance in South Korea’s Kospi. Those markets took a beating last week, led by losses in AI-related shares.
Elsewhere, Chinese stocks were up 0.3%. Gold was largely unchanged near $4,180, while the Dollar Index held near Friday’s lows, below 102.
China’s gross domestic product (GDP) grew 4.5% year on year in the third quarter, according to data from the National Bureau of Statistics released Monday. That was faster than the second quarter’s 4.3% pace. Other data also pointed to stronger domestic demand in the world’s second-largest economy. Retail sales of consumer goods rose 1.1%, more than double the 0.5% increase expected and up from 0.4% the previous month.
China is the world’s factory, its second-largest economy and a major importer of industrial commodities. Strong economic data from the country therefore tends to encourage risk-taking across financial markets.
The rebound is also consistent with the VIX’s historical tendency to normalize after Friday spikes, a pattern that has often coincided with steadier equity markets.
Oil prices fell on both sides of the Atlantic, reversing some of last week’s gains. Reuters attributed the decline to expectations that President Donald Trump’s Russia waiver would boost supply. Still, geopolitical risks in the Middle East persist.
A sustained decline in oil could ease inflation fears, clearing the way for the Federal Reserve to cut interest rates. As of this writing, the central bank is expected to keep its benchmark borrowing cost unchanged in the 4.75% to 5% range this month. It raised rates by 25 basis points last month.

reference_summary: Bitcoin rose to around $83,000 as Asian stocks and contracts tracking the Nasdaq gained on Monday, following stronger Chinese economic data and falling oil prices. China's economy grew 4.5% from a year earlier in the third quarter, and retail sales rose 1.1%, more than double the expected increase. The rebound followed technology-led market losses the previous week.

title: XRP Ledger is set to fix its lending code before anyone can use it
article_text:
XRP Ledger is set to fix its lending code before anyone can use it. XRP Ledger is set to fix its lending code before anyone can use it
Validators have a bug-fix patch on course to go live Friday. The lending system it partly repairs is still 10 votes short of approval.
- A package of XRP Ledger bug fixes is expected to take effect around 09:34 UTC on Oct. 23 after securing the minimum 29 validator votes required for approval.
- The fixes address Ripple’s proposed uncollateralized lending system, which remains inactive because its lending and vault amendments have only 19 and 21 votes, respectively.
- The package also closes a loophole that could allow certain accounts to create tokens despite having permission only to destroy them, while revising vault rounding and loan-default rules.
A batch of bug fixes is set to go live on the XRP Ledger on Friday, and some of them patch the lending system Ripple has pitched to banks and payment companies since June — a system that hasn’t been switched on yet and is still 10 votes short of approval.
Validators are the independent servers that agree on which transactions count. A change to the network’s rules needs backing from more than 80% of the 35 validators the network trusts by default, which works out to 29, and that backing has to hold for two straight weeks.
Under the plan, a lender deposits XRP or another token into a vault, and a loan broker lends that money out for a fixed term. The ledger records the loan and tracks repayments, and the broker decides offchain whether a borrowe
Borrowers don’t post collateral, so the broker’s judgment is all that stands between lenders and a default. Ripple has pitched the setup to payment companies that need cash while a cross-border settlement clears.
The bug-fix package, called fixCleanup3_4_0, had exactly 29 votes as of Monday, according to the XRPL Dashboard. It’s nine days into its two-week countdown and on course to go live around 09:34 UTC on Oct. 23. It has no votes to spare, so one validator pulling support would restart the clock.
The lending system has 19 votes. The vaults that would hold lenders’ money are a separate change and have 21. Neither has started a countdown, so even if both hit 29 votes today, lending couldn’t go live before early November.
Separately, the patch also closes a loophole that could let an account allowed only to burn, or destroy, tokens on an issuer’s behalf create new ones under certain conditions, according to the xrpld 3.4.0 release notes.
It will further changes how vaults round amounts and how the lending code decides when a loan is late or in default.

reference_summary: An XRP Ledger software update is expected to take effect on October 23, fixing bugs in Ripple's proposed lending system and a loophole that could let some accounts create tokens without permission. The lending service, which would let borrowers obtain loans without pledging assets as security, remains inactive because it lacks enough approval votes from the servers that verify transactions. The bug fixes have the minimum votes required, but losing one vote would restart their approval countdown.

title: Zcash developers plan a fix to keep ZEC swaps private from future quantum computers
article_text:
Zcash developers plan a fix to keep ZEC swaps private from future quantum computers. Zcash developers plan a fix to keep ZEC swaps private from future quantum computers
The team behind Zakura wants every swap through NEAR Intents to get its own key, so a refund address left on NEAR’s public chain can’t expose a user’s wider payment history.
- Zakura wants to assign a separate viewing key to every ZEC swap made through NEAR Intents, limiting the payment history that a future quantum computer could uncover from a publicly posted refund address.
- The proposal would keep spending keys with users while using private information retrieval to help wallets locate refunds without revealing which addresses they are checking.
- Zakura says compatible software wallets could adopt the open-source feature within weeks, before Zcash developers’ January target for quantum-resistant payments.
Zcash is designed to make crypto payments private. But a future quantum computer could theoretically exploit a small gap in NEAR Intents, a cross-chain swapping service, to connect a user’s private ZEC transactions to their wallet, undermining that privacy.
Fortunately, the team behind Zakura, a newer version of the software that runs the Zcash network, is taking steps to address that. In a new engineering post, it proposed giving every ZEC swap made through NEAR Intents its own private key. The change would close a gap that a future quantum computer could use to piece together a user’s payment history.
NEAR Intents is a service that lets users swap tokens across different blockchains. When someone swaps private ZEC for USDC through it, the service posts one of their private Zcash addresses on NEAR’s public chain, so it knows where to send back any unused ZEC. That address goes up as soon as the deposit lands and stays there even if the swap goes through and no refund is ever needed.
Such addresses give away no information on today’s computers. Each Zcash address carries a public key built from the wallet’s viewing key, the secret a wallet uses to spot payments sent to it, using one-way elliptic-curve math similar to what protects bitcoin and ether wallets.
Ordinary computers can’t run that math in reverse, but a large enough quantum computer running Shor’s algorithm, a method published in 1994 for exactly that job, could theoretically work backward from the address to the key.
That’s the real threat hanging over Satoshi-era bitcoin, whose public keys already sit onchain for anyone to copy. Last week, Google said its Willow quantum chip had produced near-perfect versions of one of the components such an attack would burn through, a step toward a machine powerful enough to try it.
Quantum computers capable of that are still likely years away (and no one has a firm timeline for when one could be built), but it’s a problem developers across the industry are rushing to solve.
One key for every swap
Zcash’s architecture creates its own problem. A Zcash wallet can generate many addresses that look unrelated, but they usually share one viewing key.
An attacker who cracks that key from a single published address could link every payment the account ever received and read the amounts and the private notes, or memos, attached to them.
Spending takes a separate key, so the funds themselves would stay safe. Zakura’s fix gives each swap its own viewing key and leaves the spending key with the user’s main account. An attacker who someday cracks a refund address on NEAR would see only the payments tied to that one swap.
The design also deals with a practical snag.
A wallet that has made hundreds of swaps would end up with hundreds of keys, and restoring it from a backup would mean scanning the entire Zcash chain with every one of them.
Zakura’s answer is a database the wallet can query privately using a technique called private information retrieval. The wallet asks where its refunds landed, and the database answers without learning which addresses the wallet asked about.
As such, no quantum computer has been demonstrated that can recover these keys. Zakura says wallets built on its open-source libraries, including Vizor, could add the feature in the coming weeks, with hardware wallets following once their firmware supports it.
That would put the fix in users’ hands ahead of the January target Zcash developers set earlier this month for quantum-resistant payments.

reference_summary: The team behind Zakura, software for the privacy-focused cryptocurrency Zcash, proposed giving each exchange of ZEC for other tokens through NEAR Intents its own key for viewing payments. This would limit how much transaction history a future powerful quantum computer could uncover from a refund address published by the swapping service, while users would keep separate keys controlling their funds. No existing quantum computer has demonstrated this attack, and Zakura says compatible wallet apps could add the feature within weeks.

title: Bitcoin whale moves $34 million in BTC it got in 2013 when coins traded at $131
article_text:
Bitcoin whale moves $34 million in BTC it got in 2013 when coins traded at $131. Bitcoin whale moves $34 million in BTC it got in 2013 when coins traded at $131
A bitcoin wallet dormant since 2013 moved 411 BTC, now worth about $34 million. It is one of several long-dormant wallets to wake up recently.
- A Bitcoin wallet dormant since 2013 transferred all 411.45 of its coins, now worth about $34 million, to a new address on Sunday.
- The owner acquired most of the Bitcoin when it was worth about $54,000 and held it through major market swings as its value increased more than 600-fold.
- The funds have not moved to an exchange, and the transfer to a modern SegWit address suggests a security upgrade rather than an imminent sale.
A bitcoin 
On Sunday, the wallet moved all 411.45 of its BTC to a new address, according to blockchain data from Arkham Intelligence. At today’s price of about $82,600 per coin, that stash is worth roughly $34 million. When the owner first acquired those coins, the entire balance was worth just $54,000.
This awakening is part of a broader trend of historic supply shifting wallets this month. Just a day prior, two other wallets dormant for over a decade moved a combined 417 Bitcoin, and the week before, a large whale wallet static since the pre-Covid crash migrated its funds.
The pattern is highly reminiscent of 2025, when isolated mega-whales repeatedly woke up from a prolonged slumber. Just like last year, these sudden movements of long-dormant supply tend to spark speculation about a potential sale. But, as was the case then, most of the coins have been moved to new private wallets, a sign of custodial maintenance rather than an impending market dump.
The specific wallet behind Sunday's move received the bulk of its funds, some 411 BTC, on Sept. 11, 2013. Back then the cryptocurrency traded around $131. Over the next 13 years, the owner didn't buy, sell, or move a single coin. They simply sat tight as the asset's value skyrocketed more than 600 times, holding through three halvings, the 2017 boom, the 2022 FTX collapse, and the launch of spot bitcoin ETFs in 2024.
While the owner remained completely inactive, the wallet itself did see some activity over the years. Dozens of tiny deposits trickled in, each worth less than a dollar. Several came from addresses that Arkham labels as phishing. It’s a common scam tactic known as “address poisoning.” Fraudsters send trace amounts of crypto ("dust") to high-value wallets, hoping the owner will accidentally copy the scammer's address from their transaction history during a future transfer.
The whale didn't fall for it.
At 18:23 UTC on Sunday, the owner sent the entire fortune to a new address, paying a transaction fee of just 337 satoshis, a fraction of a single cent.
So far, the funds have not been moved to an exchange. The new destination wallet has only received this single transfer and has not initiated any outgoing transactions. That lack of movement points to routine custodial housekeeping rather than a market sell-off.
The original 2013 wallet relied on an outdated address format, whereas the new destination utilizes SegWit (P2WPKH type), which is the modern standard that offers better security and lower transaction fees. Long-dormant holders frequently migrate to these upgraded formats to secure their assets before making any major financial moves.
reference_summary: A Bitcoin wallet inactive since 2013 transferred all 411.45 of its bitcoin, now worth about $34 million, to a new address on Sunday, according to Arkham Intelligence data. Most of the coins were received when bitcoin traded near $131 and the holdings were worth roughly $54,000. The funds have not moved to an exchange, and the article suggests the newer address may reflect a wallet security upgrade rather than a sale.

title: Crypto vault deposits top $10 billion as lending risks draw regulatory scrutiny
article_text:
Crypto vault deposits top $10 billion as lending risks draw regulatory scrutiny. Crypto vault deposits top $10 billion as lending risks draw regulatory scrutiny
Curator-managed lending strategies are attracting institutional capital, while exposing depositors to collateral, liquidity and smart-contract risks.
- Crypto vault deposits have grown from $4 billion at the start of last year to more than $10 billion, according to the Financial Times.
- Vault curators select lending strategies, set risk limits and collect fees, performing a role similar to traditional fund managers.
- U.S. and European regulators are examining oversight as hacks, illiquid collateral and automatic liquidations expose investors to potential losses.
Crypto lending vaults have attracted more than $10 billion in deposits, as investors seek returns on their digital assets, according to the Financial Times.
Deposits have risen from $4 billion at the start of last year, highlighting growing demand for strategies that put stablecoins and other tokens to work.
Vaults operate through smart contracts on decentralized finance platforms. Each has a “curator”, effectively an investment manager, who selects lending strategies, sets risk limits and collects fees. Returns typically range from 3% to 10%, although riskier strategies can generate as much as 20% or more.
The appeal comes with considerable risks. Loans can be backed by illiquid tokens, crypto-backed stablecoins or tokenized private credit, leaving depositors exposed if collateral loses value or becomes difficult to sell.
Automatic liquidations can intensify market declines, while hacks, coding errors and flawed pricing mechanisms create additional vulnerabilities. Publicly accessible smart contracts offer transparency, but investors may focus on headline yields without understanding the underlying exposure.
Fintech companies, digital asset treasury businesses and hedge funds are among the main depositors, according to the article.
Bitcoin backed lender Two Prime are among the firms entering the market. In September, it rolled out a bitcoin lending vault on Pareto targeting annual yields of 1.5% to 2% through institutional lending. The vault accepts wrapped bitcoin, requires a minimum deposit of 5 WBTC and has roughly $10 million of Two Prime’s capital committed to absorb initial losses.
Regulators are examining whether existing rules should apply. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission has raised questions about vaults holding securities, while European regulators have proposed oversight of intermediaries providing access to DeFi.
reference_summary: Deposits in cryptocurrency lending vaults have grown from $4 billion at the start of last year to more than $10 billion, according to the Financial Times. These services use computer programs to lend deposited assets, while managers choose strategies and risk limits in return for fees. U.S. and European regulators are examining oversight because depositors can lose money through hacks, software errors or loans backed by assets that fall in value or are difficult to sell.

title: JPMorgan's JPM Coin, representing dollar deposits, is coming to Ethereum: Bloomberg
article_text:
JPMorgan's JPM Coin, representing dollar deposits, is coming to Ethereum: Bloomberg. JPMorgan brings JPM Coin, representing dollar deposits, to Ethereum
JPMorgan's dollar deposit token is heading to Ethereum as the lender looks to offer it to wider selection of institutional clients.
- JPMorgan made JPM Coin, a token representing dollar deposits at the bank, available to institutional clients on Ethereum.
- Ethereum’s liquidity makes it attractive for crypto companies seeking blockchain payments and financial firms settling trades or backing tokenized assets, the bank told Bloomberg.
- The move expands JPMorgan’s blockchain efforts beyond its private Kinexys network, which processes more than $7 billion in transactions daily, and the Ethereum layer-2 network, Base.
JPMorgan(JPM), the largest U.S. bank, brought its almost year-old crypto token, JPM Coin, to Ethereum as part of a plan to expand beyond Base, the layer-2 blockchain built by Coinbase Global 
JPM Coin, which represents dollar deposits at the bank, was technically deployed on the Ethereum mainnet on Monday and is available for institutional clients’ use, the bank said in an emailed statement.
The bank chose Ethereum because the blockchain offers more liquidity than rival networks and is already used by institutional clients, Emma Landriault, the head of Kinexys Labs at JPMorgan’s blockchain division Kinexys, said in an interview with Bloomberg, which reported the news earlier.
“Issuing JPM Coin first on Base and now on Ethereum is a meaningful step towards providing our institutional clients with multi-chain optionality for moving wholesale money across both the web3 and traditional finance ecosystems,” she said in the emailed statement.
The banking giant flagged a move outside Base back in January, saying it was planning to take the token to the Canton Network. Broadening its availability aims to serve crypto firms that want to make blockchain payments and financial firms that need a digital token to settle trades or back tokenized assets, Landriault said.
Tokenization is the process of converting real-world assets and financial assets into a digital form that’s recorded and traded on a decentralized ledger. The advantage is speed, including faster settlement of trades, quick movement of money while bypassing delays and frictions involved in traditional rails.
Banks have embraced tokenization, but mostly away from public networks. In the U.S., JPMorgan, Citi (C), Bank of America (BAC) and Wells Fargo (WFC), along with more than a dozen other banks, have plans to start a shared network for tokenized deposits.
JPMorgan’s private blockchain network, Kinexys, already handles more than $7 billion a day, a small piece in the bank’s $12 trillion a day payments business. Almost $50 billion worth of crypto assets are locked in Ethereum-based applications, according to DeFiLlama.
Abroad, JPMorgan is among more than 30 banks that are helping Swift, the interbank messaging service, define the features and governance of its blockchain-based ledger. In July, Swift said 17 banks, including Citi and Wells Fargo, were preparing to pilot live transactions on it. JPMorgan wasn’t on that list.
