title: JPMorgan sees 10% annual bitcoin returns, topping stocks, bonds and gold over next decade
article_text:
JPMorgan sees 10% annual bitcoin returns, topping stocks, bonds and gold over next decade. JPMorgan sees 10% annual bitcoin returns, topping stocks, bonds and gold over next decade
The report marks the first time JPMorgan has put a range on bitcoin returns in its research, though the bank remains cautious about BTC's role in portfolios.
- JPMorgan Asset Management projects bitcoin will return 10% annually over the next decade in its base case, outpacing its forecasts for U.S. stocks, bonds and gold.
- The asset manager’s first range of long-term bitcoin forecasts spans from a 9.7% annual loss in its bear case to a 17% annual gain in its bull case.
- JPMorgan remains cautious about bitcoin, describing it as a speculative asset whose volatility and unstable correlations hinder its widespread inclusion in investment portfolios.
JPMorgan’s (JPM) asset management division expects bitcoin 
The asset manager forecasted a base case of 10% annualized returns for bitcoin over the next 10 years in its 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions report on Tuesday. The bank also set a bear case of -9.7% and a bull case of 17%.
The figure compared to projected 5.6%-6.6% growth in U.S. bonds, 7.5% and 7.7% in U.S. large and small-cap equities respectively and 5.5% in gold.
The report marks the first time JPMorgan has put a range on bitcoin returns in its research.
The New York based banking group has a complicated history with cryptocurrency, largely due to the association of CEO Jamie Dimon’s widely publicized views of bitcoin. Dimon famously described the world’s largest crypto as a “fraud” in 2017, a skeptical position he has reiterated with somewhat softer verbiage in recent years.
JPMorgan Asset Management maintained a cautious view of bitcoin in Tuesday’s report, saying its “volatility and unstable correlation to other asset classes…remain an obstacle to [its] widespread inclusion in portfolios.”
Furthermore, JPMorgan does not make a case for bitcoin as a portfolio diversifier, instead viewing it as a “speculative asset and a hedge against monetary easing,” according to comments by portfolio manager Dr Sheena Shah and head of digital asset strategy Dennis Cristallo.
“It lacks a strategic role in portfolios other than as a bet on fiat currency expansion or future asset trading on blockchains,” they added.
“BTC mostly trades like a high beta risk asset that tracks global money supply growth, but it is sometimes treated as ‘digital gold.’ Unstable correlations with other assets present a modeling hurdle. A further challenge is forecasting an asset whose fundamentals are not cash flows and whose economics may be as much about adoption, regulation and liquidity as technology.”
UPDATE (Oct. 20, 13:15 UTC): Updates to specify report is published by JPMorgan Asset Management.
reference_summary: JPMorgan Asset Management projects bitcoin could gain an average of 10% a year over the next decade in its central forecast, above its forecasts for U.S. stocks, bonds and gold. Its alternative scenarios range from an annual loss of 9.7% to an annual gain of 17%. The firm still describes bitcoin as speculative and says its sharp price swings and changing relationship with other investments limit its role in investment portfolios.

title: BlackRock seeks to shield bitcoin investors from losses after rival fund weathers 50% crash
article_text:
BlackRock seeks to shield bitcoin investors from losses after rival fund weathers 50% crash. BlackRock seeks to shield bitcoin investors from losses after rival fund weathers 50% crash
BlackRock's proposed fund follows similar products from Calamos that helped investors avoid steep losses during bitcoin's selloff.
- BlackRock filed Monday to offer a bitcoin-linked ETF that seeks to limit losses while allowing investors to benefit from price gains.
- Calamos' protected bitcoin ETF lost just 1% since October 2025, even as bitcoin tumbled more than 50% from its peak.
- The filing follows BlackRock's June introduction of a bitcoin income ETF as the firm expands beyond funds that track bitcoin's price.
While bitcoin 
The Naperville, Illinois-based firm's Bitcoin Structured Alt Protection ETF – October (CBOO) dropped just 1% since the start of its one-year protection period in October 2025, according to a Calamos spokesperson. The largest cryptocurrency, in contrast, tumbled as much as 52% from its record high of roughly $126,000.
Now BlackRock (BLK), the world's largest asset manager, wants to offer investors a similar way to protect themselves from bitcoin's price swings.
On Monday, the firm filed to introduce the iShares Bitcoin Managed Protect ETF, which would give investors exposure to bitcoin's gains while seeking to limit losses when the cryptocurrency falls.
"The Fund seeks to provide upside exposure to the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF and/or similar bitcoin exposure up to an approximate limit, while seeking to provide a level of downside protection," BlackRock said in the filing.
The proposed fund would build on BlackRock's flagship iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT), which manages more than $65 billion in assets and is the largest of the U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs introduced in 2024.
BlackRock, based in New York City, isn't breaking new ground.
Calamos debuted its first three protected bitcoin ETFs in early 2025, offering investors a choice between full downside protection and funds that limit losses to 10% or 20% over a set period.
BlackRock’s filing did not provide details on how much downside protection the proposed fund would offer, nor how much of bitcoin's upside investors could capture.
Calamos puts roughly 90% of the funds' assets into U.S. Treasuries and uses the rest to buy bitcoin-linked options. The structure allows investors to benefit when bitcoin rises, up to a set cap, while limiting losses over a defined period.
The strategy has found an audience. Matt Kaufman, Calamos' head of ETFs, said in May that the protected bitcoin funds had attracted between $10 million and $15 million over several weeks, even as spot bitcoin ETFs saw outflows.
BlackRock has also been looking beyond funds that track bitcoin's price.
In June, it launched the Bitcoin Premium Income Fund (BITA), which holds bitcoin and IBIT shares while selling call options on roughly 25% to 35% of its portfolio to generate monthly income.
"There are investors across the spectrum ... looking to generate some amount of income off of still having a mostly large, mostly long position to bitcoin," Jay Jacobs, BlackRock's U.S. head of equity ETFs, told CoinDesk at the time.
reference_summary: BlackRock applied to launch a bitcoin-linked investment fund that aims to limit losses while allowing gains up to a cap. The filing follows similar Calamos products, including one that lost about 1% during its one-year protection period despite bitcoin falling as much as 52% from its peak. BlackRock has not yet specified how much protection its proposed fund would offer or how much of bitcoin's gains investors could receive.

title: Kazakhstan court bars Coinbase, five others from unlicensed crypto services in Astana International Financial Centre
article_text:
Kazakhstan court bars Coinbase, five others from unlicensed crypto services in Astana International Financial Centre. Kazakhstan court bars Coinbase, five others from unlicensed crypto services in Astana International Financial Centre
The court injunctions apply strictly to users within the AIFC and do not extend across the rest of Kazakhstan.
- Kazakhstan’s AIFC Court barred Coinbase and five other crypto exchanges from offering unlicensed services inside the Astana financial center.
- The court injunctions apply strictly to users within the AIFC and do not extend across the rest of Kazakhstan.
- LBank was removed from the order after resolving AFSA concerns, while Apple and Google face potential app-store duties once served.
Kazakhstan’s financial regulator secured court orders restricting Coinbase and five other crypto platforms from offering services without authorization in the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC).
The Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA) said that the injunctions cover BingX, Bitcoin.com, Huobi Global (HTX), BitMart, Coinbase and WEEX. The orders prohibit the platforms from offering or marketing unlicensed digital asset services and distributing mobile apps for those services within the center.
The restrictions do not amount to a nationwide ban. In a Sept. 15 judgment, Justice Sir Stephen Richards said the injunctions apply only to the AIFC and users located there.
The Astana International Financial Centre is a financial hub in Kazakhstan’s capital that operates under its own legal framework and regulator. It requires crypto firms to obtain a license to offer services within the center.
The order also binds Google and Apple as app-store operators, though the court declined to issue a separate injunction against them, saying AFSA should first discuss necessary steps with the firms.
LBank was named in the initial proceedings, and was removed on Sept. 18 after addressing AFSA’s concerns. The regulator said the platform blocked access to its services in Kazakhstan.
The court entered judgment by default after the platform operators failed to respond within the required period. AFSA said its enforcement effort began in 2025 with warnings to more than 20 crypto platforms, followed by court proceedings in early 2026.
Coinbase had previously faced restrictions in Kazakhstan in 2023, when authorities blocked its website over alleged violations of the country’s digital asset law.
CoinDesk reached out to the platforms for comment, but hadn’t heard back before publication.
reference_summary: A court barred Coinbase and five other cryptocurrency platforms from offering or marketing unlicensed services within Kazakhstan's Astana International Financial Centre, a financial hub with its own regulator and legal framework. The restrictions apply only to users inside that center. LBank was removed from the proceedings after addressing the regulator's concerns, while the platforms still covered by the orders had not responded to the case in time.

title: The Coinbase allegations expose Bitcoin's corporate governance gap
article_text:
The Coinbase allegations expose Bitcoin's corporate governance gap. The Coinbase allegations expose Bitcoin's corporate governance gap
Corporate adoption of bitcoin will stall as long as companies can't show who controls the money, who approves its movement, or whether it's still there, argues Onramp CEO Michael Tanguma.
BlockTower Capital founder Ari Paul publicly accused Coinbase of losing roughly $25 million of his firm's assets and concealing hacks totaling more than $1 billion across a dozen institutions. Coinbase flatly denies it, Paul says active litigation prevents him from publishing his evidence, and the industry has spent the weeks since arguing about who is telling the truth.
The argument misses the most uncomfortable fact in the story: nobody outside the two parties involved can check. That is a strange place to land for an industry built on an asset designed so that no one would have to take anyone's word for anything. A custodian holding assets for much of the market stands accused of billion-dollar concealment, and the only tools available for evaluating the claim are the accuser's credibility and the custodian's word. The lesson for every company holding bitcoin, or deciding whether to, is that bitcoin on a balance sheet presents a controls problem, and until a custody arrangement can answer the same questions a board asks about the company’s bank and brokerage accounts, who can move the money and who signs off, stories like this one will stay unanswerable.
The questions no board can answer
Every other account a company touches comes with governance as a default. A corporate bank account has named users, defined roles, approval rules on withdrawals and an audit trail that a controller can hand to an auditor. A brokerage account has the same. The moment a business buys bitcoin, all of that disappears into one of two places: a single exchange login or a hardware wallet in somebody's drawer.
Boards have noticed, and they’re asking questions. Who can move the asset? Who approves the movement? What happens when the person holding the credentials quits, gets phished, or dies? These are not hypotheticals. QuadrigaCX’s chief executive died in 2018, holding the only keys, and roughly $190 million in customer assets went with him, as the Ontario Securities Commission later documented. Prime Trust discovered in December 2021 that it could not open its own legacy wallets, and still could not 18 months later when Nevada moved to put it into receivership. Across most of the industry, the honest answer to all these questions is a shrug. Companies that wanted bitcoin on the balance sheet have walked away at exactly this point. When Deloitte asked 200 CFOs at billion-dollar companies what was holding them back, the complexity of accounting and controls came in at 42%, within a point of price volatility. The asset was rarely the hard part.
The problem is more acute now than at any point in Bitcoin's history, because the threat landscape is compounding from two directions. Bitcoin turns holders into physical targets, and that hasn't waited for a new price high. Jameson Lopp's public tracker now logs more than 360 known physical attacks since 2014, including 86 in 2025 and more than 60 so far this year. Coinbase made the risk concrete last year when criminals bribed its support staff and stole customer data, including names, addresses and balance information. The company estimated the breach could cost $400 million; security researchers called it a wake-up call because stolen account data exposes holders to real-world coercion.
On the digital side, artificial intelligence has industrialized the attack: cloned voices on the phone with the finance team, phishing emails indistinguishable from the chief executive's, social engineering that improves monthly. A business holding a bearer asset on a single credential carries that entire surface area on behalf of its employees and owners, for an asset where losses are often permanent.
Why the current fixes fail
The industry's existing answers all concentrate risk instead of distributing it. Self-custody concentrates it on one person, which is why corporate self-custody collapses into key ceremonies at every hire and departure and a controller praying the keyholder never leaves angry. Exchange custody concentrates it on one company, with the client holding neither the keys nor any way to see behind the login. Audits, trust charters and SOC reports test the custodian's own books and processes. None of them gives the client named users, approval rules on withdrawals, or a way to confirm the asset is there without asking. The shutdown of BitMEX after 11 years was a reminder of how routinely single institutions simply end. Proof-of-reserves attestations, the industry's favorite half measure, show a snapshot of assets without showing controls, and say nothing about who can move what tomorrow.
The durable fix uses properties bitcoin already has. Multiple signatures are native to the protocol, which means keys can be generated and held by independent regulated institutions, with no single institution able to move or lose the asset, the company holding legal title, named users with defined roles, approval policies on every withdrawal, and an audit trail a board can actually read.
Institutions are already moving in this direction. When Morgan Stanley designed custody for its proposed bitcoin ETF, it named two custodians rather than one, a sign that relying on a single custodian is now a live concern at the top of the market. But splitting custody only goes halfway. The real test is whether the owner can see for itself what it holds, without taking any custodian's word for it. Bitcoin makes that possible, and a custody setup that doesn't take advantage of it leaves the owner exactly where Coinbase's clients are today, waiting for someone to tell them the truth.
Single-custodians are, admittedly, convenient
The fair objection is that single-custodian arrangements exist for good reasons. They're simple: one counterparty to vet, one contract, one integration, and for many companies that simplicity is worth a lot. Spreading custody across independent institutions is harder than it sounds, requiring coordination, shared standards and operational discipline the industry spent its first 15 years avoiding.
Both points are true, and neither weakens the case. Simplicity is only an advantage if what's being simplified can be checked. A single custodian that can't show its clients what it holds hasn't removed complexity; it has hidden it. The cost of that only shows up when a question like the one facing Coinbase lands, and nobody outside can answer it. A financial system in which a billion-dollar question about client assets can't be settled from the outside has failed at the exact thing bitcoin was invented to fix. Building something better than a single point of trust is hard, and it's also the industry's actual job.
Verification was the whole point
Corporate adoption of bitcoin will stall as long as companies hold it in custody that can't show who controls the money, who approves its movement, or whether it's still there, which is exactly the gap the Coinbase allegations exposed. Boards do not need to become bitcoin experts to force the change; they only need to ask what they already ask of every other account, and add one more question: what survives the departure of any single person or institution. Any custody arrangement that cannot answer those questions clearly is a risk disclosure waiting to be written. A decade from now, the industry will look back with astonishment that it invented a radically new form of money and spent years custodying it behind a single login. The sooner custody is built so that no single party can lose, move, or lie about what it holds, the sooner the question hanging over the industry becomes impossible to ask.
Note: The views expressed in this column are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of CoinDesk, Inc. or its owners and affiliates
reference_summary: BlockTower founder Ari Paul accused Coinbase of losing about $25 million of his firm's assets and hiding more than $1 billion in hacks affecting institutions, allegations Coinbase denies. In this opinion column, Onramp CEO Michael Tanguma argues that the dispute exposes companies' difficulty independently checking their bitcoin holdings and who can move them. He advocates systems requiring approval from multiple independent institutions, clear staff permissions and records of withdrawals.

title: Ripple brings Wall Street into 24/7 stock bets, but HSBC warns markets are still thin
article_text:
Ripple brings Wall Street into 24/7 stock bets, but HSBC warns markets are still thin. Ripple brings Wall Street into 24/7 stock bets, but HSBC warns markets are still thin
Institutions can trade through Ripple Prime and post RLUSD as collateral. Finding enough buyers and sellers for large positions could prove harder.
- Ripple Prime now allows institutional clients to trade swaps tied to more than 100 stock, commodity and currency markets around the clock, using its RLUSD stablecoin as collateral.
- HSBC called the offering “evolutionary, not revolutionary,” warning that limited liquidity could constrain large trades and initially favor market makers, proprietary traders and hedge funds.
- The risks of weekend trading surfaced when nearly $52 million in leveraged chip-stock positions were liquidated within 10 minutes while the underlying shares were not trading.
Ripple is giving institutions a way to bet on stocks, gold and oil over the weekend through its brokerage business, but HSBC says thin trading could limit how much money follows them in.
Daragh Maher, head of digital assets research at HSBC, called the launch an “evolutionary, not revolutionary” step in a note to clients on Monday, a copy of which was shared with CoinDesk.
“This is a rapidly growing market but not a very big one when compared to the Trad Fi markets they are tracking,” Maher wrote. “The stronger case for the product comes once there is sufficient depth for investors to express views and adjust risk when conventional markets are closed.”
Ripple Prime, the brokerage formerly known as Hidden Road, now lets clients trade swaps tied to more than 100 markets, including shares, commodities and currencies. A swap is a contract that pays out according to price movements, letting a client take a position without buying the underlying asset. Trading firm Virtu is already using the service, Ripple said in its Oct. 15 announcement.
The swaps track perpetual futures listed by Trade.xyz, a platform for stock and commodity contracts on Hyperliquid, a crypto derivatives exchange. Perpetuals have no expiry date and trade around the clock, letting a fund take a position on gold on Sunday while conventional markets are closed.
Clients deal with Ripple Prime, which manages their collateral and risk across positions, and can use Ripple’s dollar-pegged RLUSD stablecoin to back their trades. Ripple had already connected its brokerage to Hyperliquid in February.
But a fund looking to trade millions of dollars still needs someone willing to take the other side at an acceptable price, and Saturday showed how quickly weekend positions can unravel.
Nearly $52 million in leveraged chip-stock positions were forcibly closed in 10 minutes as selling spread from Binance to Hyperliquid. The shares themselves weren’t trading, leaving the contracts without fresh stock-market prices to follow, and exposing risks of participating in these newfound markets.
Read More: Chip-stock bets lost $52 million in 10 minutes with Wall Street shut
Meanwhile, HSBC expects early activity to lean toward firms trading price differences between markets.
“Until that depth develops, though, activity is more likely to be concentrated among market makers, proprietary traders, and hedge funds pursuing basis trades than among institutions seeking strategic hedges,” Maher wrote. Basis trades try to profit from price gaps between related positions, such as a contract and the asset it tracks.
The bank said Ripple’s success would depend on whether the service is cheaper, simpler and makes better use of clients’ collateral than existing brokers and venues.
Ripple is already earning fees financing leveraged stock bets, as CoinDesk reported this month, expanding into a business long dominated by banks.
The new swaps are offered through Ripple Prime’s British Virgin Islands license, with more jurisdictions planned. Ripple has named an early customer but hasn’t disclosed how much the service has traded.
Read More: Ripple is earning fees financing leveraged stock bets, a business long run by banks
reference_summary: Ripple Prime now lets institutional clients trade contracts tied to more than 100 stock, commodity and currency markets around the clock without buying the underlying assets. Clients can use Ripple's RLUSD, a digital currency designed to track the U.S. dollar, as security for their trades. HSBC warned that too few buyers and sellers could make large trades difficult and initially limit activity mainly to specialist trading firms.

title: Solana’s Alpenglow, its biggest network overhaul since 2020, goes live Wednesday
article_text:
Solana’s Alpenglow, its biggest network overhaul since 2020, goes live Wednesday. Solana’s Alpenglow, its biggest network overhaul since 2020, goes live Wednesday
Alpenglow will replace the voting system Solana has used since 2020, targeting roughly 150-millisecond finality after months of testing that included a failed migration and rollback.
- Solana’s Alpenglow upgrade is expected to reduce transaction finality to about 150 milliseconds from roughly six seconds by moving validator voting off-chain.
- Faster finality could make trading and payments feel more like those on centralized exchanges, while validator costs are expected to fall by about 60 percent.
- The upgrade is scheduled to activate Wednesday after six test-network restarts and a failed migration that was later successfully completed.
Solana transactions could soon become irreversible in just 150 milliseconds, or roughly 40 times faster than today, as the network switches on its Alpenglow upgrade on Wednesday.
The upgrade changes how validators, the computers that process transactions and vote on which ones are valid, agree with each other.
Today, every validator writes its votes straight onto the blockchain like any other transaction, and a payment isn’t locked in until enough of them stack up — which takes about six seconds.
Alpenglow pulls that voting off the chain and bundles votes into certificates that can lock in a transaction in one or two rounds. If the 150-millisecond target holds up on mainnet, a Solana transaction would be settled in less time than it takes to blink.
Six seconds is a long time in a fast market, where a price can move before a trade is locked in, and exchanges and payment apps make users wait before treating a deposit as done.
But cutting that to a fraction of a second gets Solana much closer to the feel of a card payment or a trade on a centralized exchange (Ethereum, by comparison, takes roughly 13 minutes to reach full finality).
"Solana's transaction count is going to look a lot lower this week, and people will ask if something's wrong. It isn't,” shared Robin Nordnes, CEO and founder of Raiku, which builds trading infrastructure on Solana, in an email.. “Most of what got counted before was validators voting, and that's off-chain now. The trading's all still there.”
“For desks, faster finality is nice, but it was never the bottleneck. Being close to where the block is built still is,” he added.
Read More: Solana is about to halve its block times as final 200-millisecond upgrade nears
Validators also get a cheaper bill. They currently burn through about 2 SOL a day on vote fees, a cost that doubled after Solana recently cut its slot times, the window each block gets, to about 200 milliseconds.
Alpenglow scraps those fees in favor of a flat entry charge called a validator admission ticket, set at 0.8 SOL per epoch, a period of about 24 hours. That’s roughly 60% cheaper.
Getting here wasn’t smooth, however.
The test network was wiped and restarted from scratch six times since launching in early May, and one attempt to migrate to the new system failed network-wide and had to be rolled back, according to a post from Galaxy Digital, one of roughly 100 validator operators on the test network. A later migration went through, clearing the way for Wednesday’s launch.
None of that put real money at risk, since it all happened on a network built for exactly that kind of breakage.
The switch is set for the start of epoch 1064 on Wednesday, with the actual change at slot 459,653,000 after a 5,000-slot transition.
The reduction comes as Solana's validator network has shrunk by nearly a third over the past year.
The number of active validators fell to 659 at the end of September from 696 three months earlier, roughly 30% below a year ago, according to Bitwise's latest staking report. The decline came even as 69% of SOL's supply was staked.
Stake has also become more concentrated. Data from Solana Compass shows that the minimum number of validators collectively controlling more than a third of staked SOL fell to 18 from 20 over the past year, while the ten largest validators' share climbed to 24.5% from 22.2%.
Bitwise attributed the decline to operating costs. Alpenglow's lower voting fees could ease the financial burden on smaller validators, though hardware, bandwidth and hosting expenses remain.
reference_summary: Solana plans to activate its Alpenglow upgrade on Wednesday, aiming to make transactions irreversible in about 0.15 seconds instead of roughly six seconds. It changes how the computers verifying transactions reach agreement and is expected to cut their voting costs by about 60%. The launch follows extensive testing, including a failed migration that was reversed before a later attempt succeeded.

Tether led a $15 million funding round in Mural, expanding the stablecoin issuer’s investments in technology that enables AI agents to handle payments.
The Series A round, which included participation from North Island Ventures and existing investors, brings New York-based Mural's total funding to $28 million, according to an emailed announcement on Tuesday.
Mural, founded by former Palantir (PLTR) engineers, provides fintechs and other platforms with infrastructure for managing accounts, payments, identity verification and regulatory compliance across traditional banking networks and blockchains. Its customers include payroll platform Deel and browser developer Opera.
The funding comes as financial technology companies explore “agentic finance,” in which AI systems can initiate and execute transactions on behalf of individuals or businesses.
Mural's infrastructure allows companies to set transaction limits, restrict counterparties and require additional approvals for larger payments, addressing questions around authorization and accountability when autonomous software moves money.
“As agents start moving money, that connection to the banks, payment networks and compliance systems the world still runs on becomes essential,” Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said in the statement.
The investment reflects Tether's growing interest in infrastructure beyond stablecoin issuance, particularly as programmable payments emerge as a potential use case for AI-powered financial services.

Mural helps companies manage accounts, payments, identity checks and regulatory requirements across banks and cryptocurrency networks. Its software also lets businesses set spending limits and approval rules for AI systems making payments on their behalf.

title: Monero futures are again heating with leverage, raising volatility risks
article_text:
Monero futures are again heating with leverage, raising volatility risks. Monero futures are again heating with leverage, raising volatility risks
Open interest has topped $300 million and price is back above $600. A similar setup was seen before January's crash.
- Monero futures open interest has surpassed $300 million, nearing January’s record of about $320 million and increasing the risk of a sharp, liquidation-driven price move.
- Open interest has also climbed to a five-week high of 515,730 XMR as monero’s spot price recently topped $600, suggesting leveraged bets are growing alongside the rally.
- A similar buildup in January preceded a 66 percent plunge, when monero fell from about $790 to below $300 as long positions were forcibly closed.
Leveraged bets are building up in monero (XMR) futures, raising the odds of a sharp, sudden move in the price.
Monero (XMR) is a cryptocurrency built for privacy. Its transactions are hard to trace and at the market cap of $10.9 billion, it is the second-largest privacy coin in the world.
Notional open interest, or the dollar value of the number of active monero futures bets, has risen past $300 million, approaching the January peak of around $320 million, according to data source SoSoValue. Futures are contracts that let traders bet on a coin’s price without owning it. To date, the tally has topped $300 million only a few times, all this year.
“The last Time we reached that amount of Open Interest was in Jan 2026. Monero Crashed 66% in the next 20 days. I Smell a very big Liquidation Event on XMR,” said pseudonymous crypto analyst Doctor Profit, who correctly called BTC’s 2025 top and pivoted to accumulation in July this year.
Open interest is tracked in dollars and in coins. Traders use the two differently. The dollar figure shows the current size of the market’s positions and lets traders compare monero with other cryptocurrencies. Liquidations are also typically reported in dollars, so a larger dollar figure points to a larger potential wave of forced selling. Open interest is also rising in coin terms. At 515.73K XMR, it is at a five-week high and up sharply from 400K XMR a week ago.
Liquidations, or forced closure of positions by exchanges, happen because futures involve leverage, in which a trader puts up a small deposit, called margin, to control a much larger position.
This leverage boosts gains when the market moves as expected, but when it doesn’t, the margin is eaten away. At some point, the exchange steps in and closes the position to prevent the trader’s losses from exceeding the collateral they posted and to protect the exchange from unpaid losses.
Traders betting on a rise, called longs, get liquidated when the price falls. The liquidation, in turn, adds to selling pressure in the market. This is especially true when most traders are long. In such cases, a slight price decline can trigger mass liquidation of longs and a price crash.
That’s what happened in January when open interest hit a record high alongside a price rise, reflecting an overcrowding of longs. The spot price hit a high of around $790 on Jan. 14. By the first week of February, it had crashed to under $300. This was characterized by liquidation of longs worth several million dollars, according to Coinglass.
This time too, the spot price has risen with the open interest. Monero recently topped $600, the highest since January.
Whether history repeats remains to be seen.
reference_summary: Outstanding contracts used to bet on privacy-focused cryptocurrency monero exceeded $300 million as its price climbed above $600. Many traders use borrowed money to enlarge these bets, creating a risk that losses will force positions to close automatically and intensify price swings. A similar buildup preceded monero's 66% fall earlier this year, but whether that pattern will repeat is uncertain.

title: Bitcoin risk management grows more popular as the 'just bet on price' era fades
article_text:
Bitcoin risk management grows more popular as the 'just bet on price' era fades. Bitcoin risk management grows more popular as the 'just bet on price' era fades
Your day-ahead look for Oct. 21, 2026
This is an excerpt from CoinDesk newsletter 'Daybook.' Sign up here, if you haven't already.
Bitcoin 
According to Volmex, the issuer of the bitcoin volatility index BVIV, options accounted for just under 60% of open interest among all bitcoin derivatives last week. That’s up from around 50% at the start of the year.
Open interest is the total value of contracts that traders have opened and not yet closed. The market encompasses bitcoin futures, perpetual futures and both bitcoin-native and ETF-based options.
Volmex called the growth a structural shift in bitcoin markets, a sign that trading bitcoin is now about managing risk, not just betting on direction.
Options allow investors to hedge their holdings, earn additional income or bet on a big move without borrowing, so positions can last longer than a leveraged perpetual bet. They are also priced on expected volatility, which is what gauges like Vomex’s BVIV track.
Options are derivative contracts with a fixed expiry date that let traders bet on three things at once. They can bet on the direction of the price, on how big the swings will be and on timing, meaning by when a move will or won't happen.
As of Friday, the bitcoin derivatives market looked like this: Options tied to U.S. bitcoin exchange-traded funds had about $36 billion in open interest, with BlackRock’s IBIT accounting for nearly $35 billion of the total. Add in options on crypto-native platforms, and the figure rises to roughly $76 billion. When bitcoin futures, including perpetual futures and dated contracts, are taken into account, the overall market reaches about $129 billion.
ETF options alone are now about 47% of the bitcoin options market, which is mainly owned by Deribit. IBIT options have tripled since January 2025, when open interest was about $11 billion.
The growth in options is consistent with the pattern seen on U.S. equities, where options tied to the S&P 500 Index accounted for nearly 75% of all derivatives linked to the index and index equivalents as of last year.
The growing use of options is also visible in BlackRock’s expanding lineup of bitcoin-related funds. In June, the world’s largest asset manager introduced the iShares Bitcoin Premium Income ETF (BITA), which seeks monthly income by selling call options on a portion of its IBIT holdings, sacrificing some upside in exchange for option premiums. This week, it filed to offer a bitcoin buffer ETF that uses options to limit losses during a downturn, while also capping potential gains.
All of this suggests bitcoin’s volatility could continue to decline, a trend that has been underway since spot bitcoin ETFs debuted in early 2024. Stay alert!

Bitcoin looks to have bounced off support at the Ichimoku cloud. For chart analysts, staying above the cloud and the 50-day moving average would signal that the bullish bias is still in place.
The immediate resistance is around $87,500, the recent high, followed by $90,000, a level with large options open interest on Deribit.

Volmex describes the change as a shift toward managing risk rather than simply betting on whether bitcoin will rise or fall. Options linked to U.S. bitcoin investment funds now make up roughly 47% of the bitcoin options market.

Dogecoin Labs will combine MyDoge, DogeOS and merchant payment tools as developers try to turn coin holders into customers for applications and businesses.
- Dogecoin Labs will combine the MyDoge wallet, DogeOS application network and Such App merchant tools to expand ways for DOGE holders to use and spend their coins.
- MyDoge says it has more than 500,000 users, while Such App already supports invoices and in-person QR payments.
- DogeOS, which remains unfinished, has opened a public test network for developers. Featured applications are listed as “coming soon,” and a proposed security link that would let Dogecoin’s network verify its applications is still in draft form.
The teams behind a Dogecoin 
Dogecoin Labs, formed in partnership with the Dogecoin Foundation, will own and operate MyDoge, DogeOS and Such App, according to an announcement shared with CoinDesk. Jordan Jefferson, founder of MyDoge and DogeOS, will lead it as CEO.
The plan connects three parts of a potential DOGE business ecosystem. Developers build applications on DogeOS, holders find them through MyDoge and merchants use Such App to accept payments. Such App’s beta already supports invoices and in-person QR payments, while its connection to DogeOS remains in the planning stage.
Dogecoin is one of the oldest cryptocurrencies, created in 2013 as a joke and featuring a shiba inu image. The token has advanced 3.9% in the past 24 hours and was recently trading around 8.2 cents.
MyDoge said it has grown to more than 500,000 users without paid acquisition. Its recently released V3 update connects the wallet to applications being built on DogeOS. The announcement does not specify how many wallet users are active or have tried those applications.
The foundation and House of Doge, its commercial arm, are contributing intellectual property and development teams. The foundation will continue its open-source development support, advocacy and community work, while Labs concentrates on products and commercial opportunities.
DogeOS opened its public test network on Sept. 30, allowing developers to build Ethereum-style lending services, exchanges and games using test DOGE. Dogecoin itself handles coin transfers, so those applications run on a separate system.
Three weeks later, DogeOS’s public user guide still marks its featured applications as “coming soon.”
Its planned security link to the Dogecoin blockchain also needs further work. DogeOS wants Dogecoin’s own network to check mathematical proofs that its applications ran correctly. A proposed rule change enabling that remains a draft. Until the link is implemented, users will have to rely on DogeOS’s selected operators and hardware to check that the applications work.

title: OCC's final rule to start fresh in weighing stablecoin rewards against GENIUS Act ban
article_text:
OCC's final rule to start fresh in weighing stablecoin rewards against GENIUS Act ban. OCC's final rule to start fresh in weighing stablecoin rewards against GENIUS Act ban
The U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency is the first of several federal agencies to finish writing regulations under the act.
- The U.S. agency that regulates national banks and trusts has issued the first final rule putting the GENIUS Act into place in January, though a number of other regulators are still working on other parts of the implementation.
- The section on stablecoin yield doesn't offer a lot of detail on what activity may fall under the law's wide prohibition of such yield from issuers, but the crypto industry has already interpreted GENIUS to permit the rewards programs that have become commonplace with stablecoin activity on exchanges.
- The final rule states that pre-existing rewards programs won't get special treatment as the OCC assesses which ones pass regulatory muster.
U.S. crypto exchanges that have long been giving people rewards for usings stablecoins will have to get the agency to sign off on those existing programs, according to the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the first federal banking regulator to issue a final rule under the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act.
The OCC, which oversees U.S. national banks and trusts that will play a central role in the issuance of stablecoins under the law, issued a final rule on Wednesday to establish the regulations under which the firms that issue the dollar-based tokens will operate — including in their third-party relationships with the exchanges on which their stablecoins change hands.
The agency — an independent bureau of the Treasury Department — has declined to offer examples or illustrations of what type of rewards operations may run afoul of the GENIUS Act, which declared that payments to customers made "solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin" won't be allowed. The industry, which won't get any safe harbors for existing programs, will just have to test the agency's case-by-case oversight to get a better sense of the rule, which is set to go live on January 18.
The regulator said it "will apply the language of the statute to the facts and circumstances of any particular arrangement." However, the agency did suggest that the word "solely" in the prohibition is carrying a lot of weight, and that a reward that "might be made, at least in part, for other reasons" would fall outside the ban in the GENIUS Act.
Payment stablecoins hew to the value of the U.S. dollar and are designed — as suggested by the name — to maintain a steady value in a crypto industry in which other assets are known to be famously volatile. The sector is currently led by Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC, but a number of entrants have begun crowding into the space.
Wednesday's extensive rule establishes the start-to-finish process for regulated firms and foreign companies to issue stablecoins in the U.S. and for how firms will keep custody of them. But the rule is also meant to operate alongside a number of similar rules still being worked on by other agencies, and this effort leaves aside the Bank Secrecy Act components that will be handled by other arms of the Treasury.
"The OCC’s final rule carries that landmark legislation forward, providing a clear, practical foundation for private-sector innovation, competition, and American leadership in digital assets,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent in a statement.
But the questions of yield have long swirled at the center of stablecoin regulation.
Yield saga
A number of financial firms, such as U.S. exchange Coinbase, have well-established rewards programs — akin to the customer incentives associated with credit card providers. Some of the highest rates are currently offered by PayPal and Kraken.
The GENIUS Act's ban on the issuers giving anything that looks like interest directly to the holders of their tokens has been a controversial topic and drew a lot of comments to the agency after its earlier proposal.
The programs have been declared by bankers to be a dangerous competitive threat to the customer deposits at the core of their business model. The banks felt so strongly about this that they lobbied to force further changes of the GENIUS Act into the later Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, and they continued fighting the point so vigorously that the Clarity Act couldn't muster unanimous Republican support when it failed to advance in a key Senate vote last month.
Without the amendments that had long been negotiated by bankers, the crypto industry, lawmakers and the White House, the unchanged GENIUS Act remains the only standard for how exchanges such as Coinbase should govern their rewards programs. Bankers who were concerned that the law's language would undermine their deposits are still stuck with that language, though bank deposits have continued to grow after the explosion of interest in stablecoins.
The new OCC rule noted that many commenters suggested the agency needed to consider that the Clarity Act may still overhaul GENIUS on this point (though odds of further action on the markets structure bill are long). But the regulator responded, "Unless and until such legislation passes, the OCC must implement the GENIUS Act’s yield prohibition, as enacted."
When the OCC first proposed its rule earlier this year, there was some uncertainty in the industry about how the agency would police the GENIUS Act's anti-evasion language meant to keep firms from gaming the restrictions on issuers from offering yield or rewards. But the industry has since embraced what it's interpreted as an ongoing legal clearance to offer certain rewards through secondary platforms.
For instance, PayPal offers a 4% return for users of its PYUSD, Coinbase One gives 3.75% on USDC positions and Kraken+ subscribers can make as much as 4.5% on USDG accounts.
"The OCC declines to presume that rewards programs that predated the GENIUS Act comply with the GENIUS Act," according to Wednesday's rule document. "The fact that Congress may have had notice of these rewards programs does not necessarily imply that Congress endorsed them as permissible."
In the final rule, it also took out what it had called "rebuttable presumptions" that assumed specified activities that would violate the rule.
Other agencies
GENIUS' implementation by regulators doesn't stop at the OCC, though that agency has influenced how others are writing their own rules. Though the GENIUS Act had called for a mid-year deadline that none of the regulators met, the Treasury Department, Federal Reserve and Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. also have rulemakings underway:
- The FDIC was first out of the gate with application standards late last year, and in April, the agency proposed its approach to regulate state-chartered institutions.
- The Treasury Department also proposed its handling of the law in August, and the industry is carefully monitoring how it will treat foreign issuers, such as Tether. That August action followed a joint proposal in April from the Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) and Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) that suggested the controls that stablecoin businesses would have to put in place, including abilities to stop or freeze transactions and compliance with the Bank Secrecy Act that governs most of the U.S. financial system.
- Just last month, the Fed issued its own proposals for member banks' subsidiaries that intend to issue stablecoins, including procedures for issuing them and standards for capital and reserves.
The overall effective date of the GENIUS Act was supposed to arrive in January, but it's unlikely all of the required rules will be in place before then, based on the scheduled periods in which the other agencies are still taking public comments.
OCC officials told reporters that the new rule will give "opportunities for a range of institutions," including community banks, to get involved with stablecoins.
The agency said it changed its reserve requirements between the proposed rule and this final one, adopting "a principles-based approach with respect to reserve asset diversification and concentration requirements," which it said is backed by requirements to "ensure a minimum amount of daily liquidity and avoid excessive concentration with respect to a single counterparty."
reference_summary: The U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued a final rule under the GENIUS Act governing stablecoins, digital currencies designed to track the dollar, scheduled to take effect on January 18. It will assess rewards programs individually against the law's ban on issuers paying customers solely for holding or using stablecoins, without automatically approving programs that already exist. Other federal agencies are still writing related rules, leaving parts of the law's implementation unfinished.

title: Crypto Long & Short: Why real-world assets need fixed-rate loans onchain
article_text:
Crypto Long & Short: Why real-world assets need fixed-rate loans onchain. Crypto Long & Short: Why real-world assets need fixed-rate loans onchain
Real-world assets already back the largest stablecoins, yet borrowing against them onchain still runs through variable-rate pools. Peter Gaffney of O2O Capital Partners explains why fixed-rate, fixed-term lending is the missing piece, and how a 5% shift in Sky and Ethena reserves could create $1.8 billion of demand for real-world assets.
You're reading Crypto Long & Short, our weekly newsletter featuring insights, news and analysis for the professional investor. Sign up here to get it in your inbox every Wednesday.
Happy Wednesday,
This is your institutional newsletter, Crypto Long & Short. This week:
- Peter Gaffney of O2O Capital Partners on what’s keeping real-world assets from scaling in DeFi
- Top headlines institutions should pay attention to by Francisco Rodrigues
- “Tron led crypto card volume in Q3 2026” in Chart of the Week
…and if you’re looking for more institutional insights: ETF Central’s Trackinsight Global ETF Survey 2026, produced with Calamos Investments and S&P Dow Jones Indices, finds nearly 7 in 10 professional investors are reassessing their ETF holdings.
Plus, CoinDesk’s latest Digital Assets Quarterly Report is out now.
Thanks for joining us!
Real-world assets need fixed-rate lending to scale in DeFi
Fixed-rate lending is the clearest growth lever for real-world assets (RWAs) in decentralized finance (DeFi). It unlocks a strategy that credit desks have run for decades but DeFi has never meaningfully implemented: buy a quality income asset, borrow against it at a locked rate below the asset’s yield and buy more of the asset. Stablecoins are steadily sitting around $300 billion in supply and aggregate vault assets are nearing the $20 billion milestone. Morpho alone carries more than $16 billion in deposits, most of it in variable-rate markets priced on pool utilization, which serve crypto-native traders who manage liquid positions in real time but leave longer-dated borrowers with uncertainty. Fixed-rate, fixed-term lending closes that gap by matching the term of the loan to the duration of the collateral, especially for RWAs whose redemptions can settle anywhere from T+7 to T+90. With the borrow cost and maturity known at entry, institutional counterparties can underwrite an RWA looping vault the same way they approve conventional term financing. This is the same bedrock foundation that formed and grew traditional credit markets to $51 trillion in US fixed income versus $1.6 trillion in floating-rate leveraged loans. The move to fixed rates is already underway: Morpho recently opened fixed-rate, fixed-term markets through Morpho Midnight, which Coinbase used to launch fixed-rate crypto-backed loans to its customers in September 2026.
DeFi is a battle-tested real-time execution engine with a narrow collateral base of volatile crypto assets that move by magnitudes in stress. This is what turned the October 10, 2025 liquidation cascade into a $19 billion event, marking the start of a nearly 60% reduction in DeFi total value locked for the eight months to follow. Expanding DeFi beyond crypto requires non-crypto-correlated RWAs, and RWAs require more precise lending markets to scale. RWAs already back the largest stablecoins, with Ethena and Sky committing more than $2.4 billion to JAAA, BUIDL, STAC, and USTB.
RWA leverage onchain runs almost entirely through variable-rate pools, where the borrow rate is set by utilization rather than by a lender agreeing to a price. Illustratively, Aave’s rate curve lifts the USDC borrow rate from 4% to 14% as utilization climbs from 92% to 100%. JAAA yields between 4.5% and 5% and Maple’s syrupUSDC pays 5.2%, while the one-year average USDC borrow rate on Aave V3 Ethereum is 4.56%, leaving just 50 basis points of spread to work with. The variance in these borrow rates scares off would-be RWA loopers or limits them to double-digit-yielding RWAs, which greatly narrows the accessible universe of investment-grade credit. Coin Metrics found routine daily utilization spikes on a $2 billion pool and the April 2026 KelpDAO rsETH exploit pinned Aave’s USDC pool at 100% utilization, causing borrowers to pay the maximum 14% rate for five days. Since tokenized credit products can take anywhere from T+1 to well beyond T+90 to settle redemptions, a spike like that can outlast the holder’s ability to exit while running an unprofitable trade.
Fixed-rate, fixed-term lending solves this because it lets the allocator match the duration of the loan to the duration of the RWA, the same way a bank extends a 70% advance at a fixed spread against investment-grade paper. Fixed-rate platforms like Tenor Finance, Kamino, Term Labs and Loopscale now quote rates against products, with a Kamino market offering 5.3% fixed-rate loans against Figure’s auto loan portfolio in rolling 30-day terms. Combined with one-click leverage providers, which compress multiple loops into a single transaction, these markets let institutional underwriters size into leveraged RWA positions at scale.
For sizing, a 5% reallocation of the $12 billion in Sky and Ethena reserve capital into fixed-rate looped RWA strategies at 3x is $600 million of equity and $1.8 billion of RWA demand, before foundations, digital asset treasury companies and exchange Earn programs contribute to growth. Well-positioned issuers of underwritten, loopable, non-crypto correlated RWAs will be the beneficiaries as DeFi’s collateral base finally grows beyond crypto.
Headlines of the week
This week’s headlines show banks further expanding blockchain payments and crypto services, while MSCI tightened index eligibility and BlackRock proposed a new way for its clients to manage bitcoin exposure.
- JPMorgan brings tokenized dollar deposits to Ethereum: The bank deployed JPM Coin on Ethereum for institutional clients, expanding beyond Base and allowing customers to use tokenized bank deposits for blockchain payments and settlement.
- Thirty-seven-bank euro stablecoin venture secures Dutch e-money license: Qivalis, backed by banks including BNP Paribas, ING and BBVA, received authorization as an electronic money institution but must complete remaining requirements under the EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) regulation before issuing its planned euro token.
- MSCI adopts rules that could remove Strategy and Metaplanet from equity indexes: New financial screens will exclude companies classified as non-operating, with affected constituents to be announced Nov. 11 and changes effective after the Nov. 30 close; neither company’s removal is yet confirmed.
- Kraken parent Payward agrees to buy Lithuania’s Saldo Bank: The acquisition would expand Payward’s European business into interest-bearing deposits, lending, card issuance and euro payments, with closing expected in 2027 subject to regulatory approvals.
- BlackRock files for a bitcoin ETF designed to cushion losses: The proposed iShares Bitcoin Managed Protection ETF (PBIT) would use options linked to the iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) to seek downside protection in exchange for limited upside, without guaranteeing investors a fixed loss limit.
Tron led crypto card volume in Q3 2026
Tron was the largest chain for crypto card volume in the third quarter of 2026 with a 27.5% share (about $638 million). The weekly share has since fallen to 23.7%, as total card volume grew and Tron’s volume held steady. Tron’s TRX has been roughly flat at $0.33 to $0.34.
For more on the Tron network, view the new CoinDesk research report on Tron.
Looking for more? Receive the latest crypto news from coindesk.com and market updates from coindesk.com/institutions.
reference_summary: Peter Gaffney of O2O Capital Partners argues that loans with fixed interest rates and repayment dates are needed to expand borrowing against stocks, bonds and other real-world assets represented on cryptocurrency networks. He says current loans with changing rates can become more expensive than the income those assets earn, while borrowers may have to wait to sell or redeem them. As a hypothetical example, he estimates that shifting 5% of Sky and Ethena's reserves into strategies using borrowed money could generate $1.8 billion in demand for such assets.

title: Bitcoin ETFs attract $1.08 billion in 3 days but it may not be enough for a steep rally
article_text:
Bitcoin ETFs attract $1.08 billion in 3 days but it may not be enough for a steep rally. Bitcoin ETFs attract $1.08 billion in 3 days but it may not be enough for a steep rally
Past steep rallies ran on about $235 million a day of net inflows into ETFs. The funds are yet to match that pace, according to data analyzed by CoinDesk.
- U.S.-listed spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds attracted more than $1 billion this week, signaling renewed but still tentative institutional demand.
- Bitcoin’s three steep rallies since January 2024 coincided with average daily ETF inflows above $200 million, compared with about $86 million a day since July 1.
- A sustained bitcoin rally may require stronger, steadier ETF inflows, though futures trading and direct purchases can also drive prices higher.
Bitcoin 
These U.S.-listed funds have pulled in over $1 billion in investor money this week, according to SoSoValue data.
Analysts are calling it a sign of renewed institutional bid for the cryptocurrency, with a warning that the pace must remain robust for a sustained uptick in bitcoin's price.
"Institutional demand shows tentative improvement. However, flows remain volatile and sustained inflows are needed to confirm a stronger recovery," Vikram Subburaj, CEO of India-based Giottus, said in an email.
History offers some support. Steep uptrends have been characterized by average daily net inflows of over $200 million.
Since the funds launched in January 2024, bitcoin has had three steep rallies, a stretch in which bitcoin gained more than 50% without ever falling more than 20% from its highest point along the way.
In the first, from Jan. 23 to March 14, 2024, bitcoin rose 79% from about $39,900 to $71,400. The funds took in an average of $294 million a day, with 10 days of $500 million or more and one of $1 billion or more.
The second ran from Aug. 5 to Dec. 17, 2024. Bitcoin gained 96%, from about $54,100 to $106,100. Daily inflows averaged $202 million, with 16 days of $500 million or more and three of $1 billion or more.
In the third, from Apr. 6 to Jul. 14, 2025, bitcoin rose 53%, from about $78,400 to $119,900. Inflows averaged $248 million a day, with 13 days of $500 million or more and two of $1 billion or more.
Across those 199 trading days, the funds took in $46.7 billion, an average of about $235 million a day. There were 39 days of $500 million or more and six of $1 billion or more.
The current pace is slower.
Since July 1, bitcoin has gained 39%, from about $60,000 to $83,500. The funds had seven days of $500 million or more in that time, about one in 11 trading days, against about one in five during the three steep rallies.
The average of about $86 million a day is well below the $200 million-plus of those steep rallies, and there hasn't been a single day of $1 billion or more.
So, if history is a guide, a steep run higher from here would require a steady pace of inflows. That said, the past is a guide, not a promise. Demand coming through other channels, such as futures or direct purchases of the token in the spot market, can also lift prices.
reference_summary: U.S. funds that hold bitcoin attracted about $1.08 billion in three days, suggesting renewed demand from large investors, although analysts say the buying remains uneven. Since July 1, daily net investment has averaged about $86 million, compared with roughly $235 million during three earlier steep bitcoin rallies. The article says stronger, steadier fund inflows may be needed for a similar rise, while noting that direct purchases and other trading activity can also lift prices.

title: Bitcoin gives back its run at $85,000 as Tesla and Meta fail to calm AI nerves
article_text:
Bitcoin gives back its run at $85,000 as Tesla and Meta fail to calm AI nerves. Bitcoin gives back its run at $85,000 as Tesla and Meta fail to calm AI nerves
BTC broke through its $84,000 ceiling late Wednesday, then slid back to the $82,500 support analysts are watching as tech futures fell.
- Bitcoin traded just below $82,800 after a brief surge to nearly $85,000 reversed, leaving the cryptocurrency near a key $82,500 support level that some analysts say could precede a slide toward $70,000.
- Most major cryptocurrencies declined, with HYPE, Dogecoin and Solana among the laggards, while Zcash gained nearly 3% and XRP edged higher.
- Disappointing corporate outlooks and renewed doubts about artificial intelligence spending weighed on U.S. stock futures and Asian markets, while oil rose amid renewed Middle East tensions.
Bitcoin was flat at just under $82,800 as of Thursday Asian morning hours after giving back a late-Wednesday surge to nearly $85,000. Mixed results from Tesla and Meta knocked Nasdaq futures lower and revived doubts about the AI trade.
ZEC was the only standout gainer among the majors, up nearly 3% to about $1,290, and XRP added less than 1%. HYPE was the laggard, down 3% to about $79. DOGE fell 2% and SOL lost about 1%, while ether, BNB and TRX slipped less than 1%, according to CoinDesk data.
The breakout didn’t last long. Bitcoin cleared $84,000, the ceiling that turned it back on Oct. 13 and 14, and topped out near $84,800 late Wednesday. Within about six hours it had dropped more than $2,000 to around $82,600, a rough night for anyone who chased the move.
That leaves bitcoin sitting on $82,500, a level that some market watchers warn could open a slide toward $70,000 if it breaks for good.
Big Tech didn’t help. Tesla fell 3% after hours after it cut its capital-spending forecast, and chip-equipment maker Lam Research dropped 7% on a weak outlook.
Meta rose 2% after raising its AI spending plans, but that wasn’t enough to lift the mood. Nasdaq 100 futures fell 1.1% and S&P 500 futures lost 0.5%.
Asia took it hard. South Korea’s Kospi dropped 2.2% as Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix retreated, and China’s CSI 300 fell 1.7%, on course for a bear market. Alibaba led Chinese e-commerce stocks lower after the government called for tighter quality control. Crude oil climbed after tensions flared again in the Middle East.
reference_summary: Bitcoin briefly approached $85,000 before falling back below $82,800 as mixed Tesla and Meta results failed to ease concerns about spending on artificial intelligence. U.S. stock-market contracts and Asian shares also declined, while oil prices rose amid renewed Middle East tensions. Most major cryptocurrencies fell, although Zcash gained nearly 3% and XRP edged higher.

title: China seeks to seize 61,800 BTC tied to $5.7 billion fraud scheme
article_text:
China seeks to seize 61,800 BTC tied to $5.7 billion fraud scheme. China seeks to seize 61,800 BTC tied to $5.7 billion fraud scheme
Chinese prosecutors are seeking to confiscate more than 61,800 Bitcoin tied to a $5.7 billion fraud scheme, days after a U.K. court ruled Chinese law governs victims’ claims to the coins.
- Chinese prosecutors are seeking to confiscate more than 61,800 BTC and other assets linked to an alleged $5.7 billion fraud that affected more than 102,000 investors.
- Prosecutors say Qian Zhimin’s company sold unlicensed wealth-management products, used investors’ money to repay earlier participants and buy assets, and left victims with nearly 20 billion yuan in losses.
- A British court ruled that Chinese law should govern victims’ claims to the Bitcoin seized in Britain, while a Chinese court has opened a six-month period for interested parties to join the confiscation case.
Chinese prosecutors have moved to seize more than 61,800 Bitcoin linked to a massive fraud case worth over 40 billion yuan, roughly $5.7 billion, according to reporting by Chinese outlet The Paper.
The case centers on Qian Zhimin, the alleged controller of Tianjin Lantian Gree Electronic Technology. Prosecutors say that from 2014 to 2017, the company sold unlicensed wealth-management products across China, promising guaranteed principal and high returns. The scheme raised more than 40.378 billion yuan from more than 102,000 investors, who lost nearly 20 billion yuan.
This money, however, was allegedly used to repay earlier investors, run fake investment projects, buy Bitcoin and acquire property, cars and jewelry, instead of funding real businesses.
Qian then fled China in 2017 and later settled in the UK. British authorities eventually seized his assets, including more than 61,800 bitcoin, plus bitcoin cash, bitcoin gold, bitcoin SV, ripple, dogecoin, cash, jewelry and investment holdings.
On Oct. 13, Tianjin’s Second Intermediate People’s Court said it had accepted prosecutors’ request to confiscate the assets as illegal gains. The court has opened a six-month period for victims and other interested parties to join the case. Victims who do not participate can still seek refunds from recovered assets.
The development comes days after a U.K. High Court ruled that Chinese law, rather than English law, should govern alleged victims’ claims to the more than 61,000 BTC seized in Britain.
The ruling doesn’t mean that victims can never recover their coins. Instead, it calls for assessing whether the victims have a property claim under Chinese law, with further hearings expected. Lawyers for some victims are seeking to appeal.
The case is one of China’s largest alleged crypto-linked frauds—and the Bitcoin stash could be worth far more today than when it was seized.

reference_summary: Chinese prosecutors are seeking to confiscate more than 61,800 bitcoin and other assets linked to an alleged $5.7 billion investment fraud involving Qian Zhimin and more than 102,000 investors. Prosecutors say investors' money was used to repay earlier participants and buy assets instead of funding genuine businesses. A U.K. court ruled that Chinese law should govern victims' claims to the bitcoin seized in Britain, while a Chinese court opened a six-month period for interested parties to join the confiscation case.

title: Asian stocks tumble, bitcoin retreats as China enters bear market

Technology shares led regional losses as mixed U.S. earnings unsettled investors and Brent crude climbed above $112 a barrel.

- Bitcoin retreats toward $82,000 as gold and silver decline, while rising oil prices add to market pressure.
Asian stocks tumbled on Thursday, with Chinese equities entering a bear market as technology shares sank and rising oil prices compounded investor concerns.
The CSI 300, which tracks the 300 largest stocks traded in Shenzhen and Shanghai, slid 2%, taking the decline from June’s peak to 20%. Other regional benchmarks followed suit. Chinese technology shares traded in Hong Kong faced their worst session since President Donald Trump’s April 2025 “Liberation Day” tariff announcement, according to Bloomberg’s David Ingles.
According to Ingles, the technology benchmark has fallen more than 40% from its peak, almost erasing gains following Beijing’s Sept. 24 stimulus package, with forward valuations compressed to roughly 13 times earnings.
Mixed third-quarter earnings reports from U.S. companies added to the uncertainty surrounding artificial intelligence investment. Tesla 
Bitcoin 
The Cboe Volatility Index, or VIX, jumped 10% to around 18, roughly 30% above September’s low. Meanwhile, WTI crude topped $100 a barrel and Brent crude climbed above $112 to the highest levels since May.

Mixed U.S. company results renewed concerns about artificial-intelligence investment, while stock indexes in Japan, South Korea and Hong Kong fell around 3% or more. Bitcoin retreated toward $82,000 and Brent oil exceeded $112 a barrel, adding to market pressure.

Led by Sam Altman, OpenAI reportedly has delayed IPO plans until 2027.

The Nasdaq lost 2.6%, and the S&P 500 was down 1.2%. The DJIA closed flat as money rotated into defensive sectors like health care and consumer staples. Dow components like JNJ, Walmart, McDonald’s, and Procter & Gamble all posted large gains for the session.
Money also found its way into the bond market, sending U.S. Treasury yields plunging 15-20 basis points across the curve.
Bond rally picks up steam as stocks slump to session lows
Money is really pouring into fixed-income as stocks extend losses two hours before the close, with the Nasdaq down 2.55% and S&P 500 losing 1.35%.
The 10-year U.S. Treasury is now down a whopping 20 basis points on the session to more than a one-month low of 4.945%. The 2-year yield is off 18 basis points to 4.64%.
October Fed rate hikes odds are more or less zero at this point, and the odds of no more rate hikes at all this year have soared to 28% from 10%.
Of particular note, interest rates are tumbling even as the price of oil has jumped more than 3% today. These markets were nearly perfectly correlated throughout the summer and early fall, with each tick higher in oil resulting in a move upward in rates.
That correlation has completely broken of late as traders reassess the idea that higher oil prices are inflationary, and instead consider the deflationary impact of the current energy shock.
Bitcoin is near a session low, down 4.2% to $81,100. Ether and XRP are each down more than 5%.
'Demand is parabolic': Blackstone's Jon Gray pushes back on AI bubble talk
“When you think about a bubble, you think about building capacity and then hoping the demand comes,” Blackstone (BX) President Jon Gray told Bloomberg. “With AI, you’re building capacity, and you’re hoping you can keep up with the demand.”
“We can’t keep up with customer demand,” he said, referring to Ode, an AI consulting company formed by Blackstone and Anthropic. “Demand is almost parabolic.”

Bitcoin BTC$77,971.30 is holding near a session low at $81,500, down 2.4% over the past 24 hours. Ether, solana, and XRP are down roughly the same amount.

title: Ethereum’s four-minute settlement plan could lower the cost of moving crypto
article_text:
Ethereum’s four-minute settlement plan could lower the cost of moving crypto. Ethereum’s four-minute settlement plan could lower the cost of moving crypto
A new draft targets a fourfold cut in the time it takes Ethereum transactions to become final, which could free up money transfer services tie up while customers’ payments clear.
- Ethereum researchers have proposed cutting transaction finality from about 16 minutes to roughly four minutes, though the unfinished plan has no activation date.
- Faster finality could reduce costs for cross-chain transfer services by allowing them to recover and reuse funds more quickly.
- The proposal would separate validators’ block-selection and finality votes, potentially enabling further speed gains and an eventual shift to quantum-resistant signatures.
Ethereum researchers want to cut the wait for a transaction to become final from about 16 minutes to roughly four, a change that could make it cheaper to move money between blockchains.
Ben Edgington, who coordinates Ethereum’s fast-finality research, filed the draft Wednesday with fellow researchers Francesco D’Amato, Roberto Saltini, Yann Vonlanthen and Mikhail Kalinin.
Its initial target is a four-fold improvement, though the design is unfinished and has no activation date.
In the current mechanism, a transaction can land in an Ethereum block well before the network treats it as final, the point where validators, the computers that secure the network, commit to never rewriting it. Anyone moving funds off Ethereum has to decide when it’s safe to release money on the other side.
But sixteen minutes is a long time to have money in limbo.
Say someone sends $10,000 from Ethereum to another network. A transfer service can pay them right away from money it already holds there, then wait to get repaid once the original transaction settles. The customer gets their funds in seconds, and the service has $10,000 tied up until Ethereum is done.
Ethereum Foundation research counts that idle money as a real cost for these firms, and a shorter wait lets them reuse it sooner. In practice, a service fronting a steady $1 million an hour would have about $267,000 waiting on repayment with a 16-minute delay. At four minutes, however, that drops to roughly $67,000.
Stablecoin providers such as Circle 
Circle also caps the total value of fast transfers waiting on final settlement, and each completed settlement frees up room for new ones.
Splitting the vote
The 16-minute wait comes down to how Ethereum’s validators vote. Each one casts a single vote that does two jobs at once, helping pick the next block and helping lock older blocks in for good. Validators take turns casting those votes, and a block only becomes final after two full rounds of everyone voting.
Both jobs share one vote so finality can only move as fast as that rotation. The proposal gives each job its own vote, so the locking-in can run on a faster clock that developers can keep tightening over time.
The researchers say splitting the votes would also make it easier to eventually swap in quantum-resistant signatures. Ethereum would need that upgrade if quantum computers ever get strong enough to break today’s cryptography.
However, four minutes would still be slow next to Solana, which switched on its Alpenglow upgrade Wednesday with a target of finality in about 150 milliseconds.
The draft leaves voting timings, penalties and parts of its security analysis unresolved as of Thursday. Edgington wrote that “many aspects remain TBD” and that the immediate aim was getting a proposal number — which puts the idea into Ethereum’s formal upgrade pipeline.
