reference_summary: Ethereum researchers proposed cutting the time before a transaction becomes irreversible from about 16 minutes to roughly four minutes. Faster confirmation could lower costs for services moving money between cryptocurrency networks by letting them recover and reuse funds they advance to customers sooner. The design remains unfinished, with important security details unresolved and no activation date.

title: Crypto for Advisors: Stablecoins are ready for prime time
article_text:
Crypto for Advisors: Stablecoins are ready for prime time. Crypto for Advisors: Stablecoins are ready for prime time
You’re reading Crypto for Advisors, CoinDesk’s weekly newsletter that unpacks digital assets for financial advisors. Subscribe here to get it every Thursday.
Happy Thursday, advisors!
In today’s newsletter, Prashant Kher of EY-Parthenon on what new survey data shows about where stablecoins are gaining ground, and what will decide which payment rails scale
Then, in “Ask an Expert,” Sam Boboev of Fintech WrapUp on whether euro stablecoins can challenge the dollar’s lead, and who is best placed to win on distribution.
Happy reading.
Stablecoins are going mainstream
A year ago, the stablecoin debate centered on whether regulatory clarity and a compelling combination of speed, cost and liquidity benefits would drive meaningful adoption. The evidence now points to a market moving decisively from experimentation toward implementation.
EY-Parthenon’s 2026 Blockchain Payments Survey of 521 corporate and financial institution decision-makers found that 18% of corporates have used stablecoins in production, double the share reported in our 2025 survey. Tokenized deposits are close behind, with 15% of corporates reporting adoption.
Financial institutions are also making firm commitments. A total of 69% offer stablecoin services or plan to launch them within two years, up from 30% in 2025. Among banks, 49% already offer or plan to offer tokenized deposits over the same period.
Although blockchain payments have not yet reached mass adoption, the survey findings provide clear evidence that the market is shifting from technology trials to integrating capabilities into existing payment workflows and treasury operations.
Cross-border payments are the entry point
Cross-border business payments remain the most common use case. Across stablecoins and tokenized deposits, 50% to 53% of all respondents have used or are exploring each for cross-border supplier payments or cross-border business-to-business (B2B) payment acceptance.
Overall blockchain payments exploration & adoption
Cross-border B2B flows lead blockchain payment use cases for most respondents, while interest in payouts is concentrated among banks and payments firms.
Source: 2026 EY-Parthenon blockchain payments survey
These applications directly address frictions corporates experience in cross-border payments. A total of 56% cite slow processing and settlement; 52% cite foreign exchange costs or spreads; 48% cite regulatory, sanctions and compliance delays; and 36% cite correspondent banking fees. Financial institutions see the corresponding opportunity, with faster settlement and lower costs ranking among the leading drivers of interest in both stablecoins and tokenized deposits.
The opportunity extends beyond basic money movement. Tokenized asset settlement was the most frequently selected opportunity to add value on top of blockchain payment rails, cited by 63% of respondents from financial institutions, reflecting strong interest in using blockchain-based money as a settlement mechanism.
The market is becoming multi-rail
Adoption is moving beyond a binary choice between stablecoins and tokenized deposits. Among respondents with an interest in blockchain payments, 45% of corporates and 53% of financial institutions favor using both rails. Respondents cite flexibility and the expectation that the two methods will coexist as leading reasons, suggesting that different payment needs will call for different forms of digital money.
That preference reflects the different roles the two methods can play. Stablecoins provide reach across wallets, platforms and public blockchain networks, while tokenized deposits can bring commercial bank money into programmable environments. Rather than selecting a single rail, organizations can choose between them based on the use case, counterparty, geography and liquidity requirements.
For financial institutions and payment providers, the opportunity is to make that choice seamless for clients, enabling them to move between payment methods, both traditional fiat and blockchain payments, through integrated processes and a unified experience.
Integration and programmability will determine what scales
Corporate expectations favor embedded delivery of blockchain payment services. A total of 76% consider integration with existing enterprise resource planning, treasury management and banking platforms very important or critical. In addition, 74% want blockchain payments fully integrated into existing banking and payment interfaces, while only 14% prefer a separate experience for digital assets.
That preference creates an advantage for incumbent providers: 63% of corporates would likely adopt blockchain payments if offered by their existing bank or payments provider. However, financial institutions must build on trusted relationships with credible economics, secure execution and regulatory readiness.
Programmability represents a separate but complementary opportunity to create value. A total of 54% of financial institutions already offer or plan to launch programmable payments within two years, and 75% view them as at least a moderate revenue opportunity. For financial institutions, the leading priorities for programmable payments include liquidity and cash management automation at 51%, conditional payments at 51%, automated reconciliation at 49% and cross-border automation at 47%.
Outlook
Blockchain payment adoption may increasingly occur inside familiar banking and payment products, rather than through stand-alone digital asset interfaces. Institutions that integrate stablecoins, tokenized deposits and traditional rails into existing workflows, while adding programmable services above those rails, will be best positioned to lead the next phase of adoption.
Disclaimer: The views expressed in this article are those of the author and not necessarily those of Ernst & Young LLP or other members of the EY global organization.
- Prashant Kher, partner, EY-Parthenon
Ask an Expert
Q. Why are payment companies launching their own stablecoins, such as OUSD, and how could this change their business models?
- Payment companies are increasingly interested in issuing stablecoins because they see an opportunity to capture more value from the money moving through their platforms.
Today, payment providers generate revenue primarily through transaction fees, currency conversion and other financial services. Issuing a stablecoin could create an additional revenue stream from the reserves backing tokens in circulation, subject to the applicable regulatory framework.
There is also a strategic benefit. A payment company with its own stablecoin could connect merchant settlements, cross-border payouts and customer balances within a single infrastructure.
This could reduce dependence on external settlement providers and improve liquidity management.
However, distribution will be critical. Issuing a stablecoin is relatively straightforward compared with convincing businesses to hold and use it.
I expect payment companies with established merchant networks and strong distribution to have an advantage. Their existing customer relationships could help them turn stablecoins into practical payment products.
Q. Why are banking consortia in the U.S. and Europe developing stablecoins, and how could they compete with existing issuers?
- Banks are increasingly concerned about losing payment flows and customer balances as stablecoin adoption grows.
In Europe, Qivalis has brought together 37 financial institutions across 15 countries to develop a regulated euro stablecoin.
Meanwhile, a separate global consortia of 21 financial institutions, including Bank of America, Citi, Goldman Sachs and Wells Fargo, announced plans in September 2026 to launch a U.S. dollar stablecoin in the first half of 2027, with euro issuance also a priority.
These initiatives could allow banks to offer around-the-clock settlement while retaining their role in managing customer funds.
I see the biggest opportunity in institutional payments and tokenized asset settlement, where banks already have established customer relationships and payment infrastructure.
However, competing with existing stablecoin issuers will require sufficient liquidity and broad distribution.
The real test will be whether these consortiums can convert their existing banking relationships into meaningful transaction volumes.
Q. What is driving the push for euro-denominated stablecoins, and can they challenge the dominance of U.S. dollar stablecoins?
- Euro stablecoins currently represent a tiny share of the market. According to Bank of Ireland, just 0.2% of global stablecoin circulation was euro-denominated in May 2026.
This creates a problem for European businesses that want to use blockchain payments while keeping their transactions and treasury balances in euros.
Using dollar stablecoins introduces foreign exchange costs and currency exposure.
The EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) regulation has provided a regulatory framework for euro stablecoin issuers, while European banks are developing infrastructure to support euro-denominated settlement.
I see the strongest opportunities in European B2B payments and corporate treasury.
However, challenging dollar stablecoins globally will be difficult. Dollar liquidity and established distribution networks give existing issuers a considerable advantage.
The more realistic opportunity is to build a strong euro stablecoin market serving European businesses and financial institutions.
Adoption will depend on liquidity and integration with existing banking systems.

- The U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency(OCC) has issued the first final rule under the GENIUS Act requiring crypto exchanges to seek approval for existing stablecoin rewards programs.
- Switzerland’s Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA) has approved the country’s first retail bitcoin fund, allowing direct bitcoin investment for everyday investors under strict risk disclosure and custody requirements.

reference_summary: EY-Parthenon's survey of 521 company and financial-institution decision-makers found that 18% of companies had used stablecoins, digital currencies designed to maintain a steady value, in live operations, double the share in 2025. Among financial institutions, 69% already offer stablecoin services or plan to within two years, up from 30% in 2025. International business payments are a leading use, and most companies want these services integrated into their existing banking and payment systems.

title: A16z is the latest VC giant to widen bets beyond crypto and into AI and emerging tech
article_text:
A16z is the latest VC giant to widen bets beyond crypto and into AI and emerging tech. A16z is the latest VC giant to widen bets beyond crypto and into AI and emerging tech
The venture investor behind early bets on Coinbase, Solana and Uniswap said is broadening its focus, joining other crypto investment firms looking beyond blockchain to artificial intelligence and tech themes.
- Prominent venture firm Andreessen Horowitz is renaming its crypto-focused arm to a16z Frontier, expanding its investment focus to artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies.
- The firm will continue investing in blockchain tech and advocating for crypto regulation while exploring autonomous machines and networks connecting people and AI agents, partner Chris Dixon said.
- The shift follows similar moves by crypto-focused venture firms, including Paradigm, Framework Ventures and Haun Ventures, to broaden their investments beyond digital assets.
Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), one of crypto's most influential venture capital backers, is dropping "crypto" from the name of its investment arm and expanding into artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies, becoming the latest major crypto investor to broaden its focus.
The Silicon Valley firm is renaming its a16z Crypto fund to a16z Frontier, targeting startups developing technologies and markets that may take years to mature, general partner Chris Dixon said in a Thursday blog post.
The move doesn't mean a16z is abandoning digital assets. The firm will continue backing crypto companies and advocating for crypto regulation, Dixon said.
"This is an expansion: we will continue to invest in crypto and related ventures and advocate for sensible crypto regulation," he wrote.
The VC giant had played a significant role in shaping the crypto industry. An early Coinbase investor, the firm also backed major blockchain projects including Solana (SOL) and decentralized exchange Uniswap (UNI), while pouring billions into crypto startups and becoming a prominent voice in U.S. policy debates.
The company’s decision is the latest example of a broader pivot among venture capital firms that made their names in crypto but are now looking beyond digital assets.
Paradigm raised $1.2 billion in July to invest in AI, robotics and other technologies, while Framework Ventures raised $400 million in June to expand into AI, energy, fintech and tokenization. Haun Ventures also broadened its focus toward AI and financial services with a $1 billion fundraising in May.
A16z Frontier will explore AI-powered products, autonomous machines and networks connecting people and AI agents. Dixon sees blockchains playing a role in those networks by enabling payments and transactions between machines.
Dixon argued that as blockchain technology spreads into mainstream finance, the distinction between crypto companies and other businesses is becoming less useful.
"Wall Street and fintech companies now regularly launch products built on blockchains,” he wrote. “Does that make them crypto companies? The label matters less now."
Dixon said he will lead the fund alongside a16z founders Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz and general partners Eddy Lazzarin and Guy Wuollet.
reference_summary: Andreessen Horowitz is renaming its cryptocurrency investment arm a16z Frontier and widening its focus to artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies. Partner Chris Dixon said it will continue backing cryptocurrency businesses and supporting clearer rules while exploring areas such as autonomous machines and networks connecting people with AI systems. The move follows similar expansions by Paradigm, Framework Ventures and Haun Ventures.

title: Senate's top Democratic investigator looking into Tether payments to Bo Hines' firm
article_text:
Senate's top Democratic investigator looking into Tether payments to Bo Hines' firm. Senate's top Democratic investigator looking into Tether payments to Bo Hines' firm
Senator Richard Blumenthal, the ranking Democrat on the investigations subcommittee, added a probe of the ex-White House crypto adviser to his list of crypto interests.
- U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal keeps digging into Tether on behalf of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, this time looking at recent reports that a firm owned by former White House crypto adviser Bo Hines took millions while he was still helping shape stablecoin policy.
- Blumenthal, the ranking Democrat on the subcommittee, sent letters to Tether and the firm, Nxum, that was co-founded by Hines, who took a job as Tether’s top U.S. executive after leaving the White House.
U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal has added another Tether probe to the many irons he has in crypto fires, this time demanding answers about reported payments the company made to a firm owned by Bo Hines — the former White House crypto adviser who is now in charge of the U.S. arm of Tether.
Blumenthal, the ranking Democrat on the Senate's Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, sent letters Thursday to Tether and to the consulting company Hines started with his father and another partner, Nxum Group.
"The highly unusual terms and nature of Tether’s business relationship with both Nxum and Bo Hines raise alarming ethical and legal concerns, indicating that Tether was likely well aware of the illegality and impropriety of issuing payments to a current White House official with such a direct role in shaping cryptocurrency legislation that was instrumental to its business," Blumenthal wrote to Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino.
The Wall Street Journal reported last week that Nxum had received large payments for consulting work for Tether when Hines was still advising President Donald Trump and his administration on crypto policy (including on stablecoin issuers significant to Tether). Blumenthal requested details of those business arrangements.
“Tether is aware of the allegations reported in The Wall Street Journal that form the basis of Senator Blumenthal’s letter,” the company said in a statement. “External counsel previously conducted an in-depth internal investigation into the matter, which found no evidence of wrongdoing.”
CoinDesk had been first to report earlier that Hines' company — which had little track record or experience in politics — was making millions of dollars as the main campaign-advertising provider for a political action committee associated with Tether.
Hines' family firm, Nxum, has recently hired another official that worked as a White House crypto adviser, Harry Jung. The office that advised Trump on crypto issues has since gone vacant, with the departure of Patrick Witt, who had replaced Hines as its executive director.
Blumenthal has been focusing significant attention on crypto, including on Trump's memecoin, crypto backers of the president's projects, Trump family crypto firm World Liberty Financial, activities at Binance and especially on Tether. He issued a report on its financial connections to Iran, and he more recently demanded answers about Tether's connection to its U.S. financial partner, Cantor Fitzgerald.
Tether's Ardoino criticized the senator's work this week, saying Blumenthal ignored important information and shared his report with the press before giving the company a look or a chance to respond.
Though Blumenthal's party has been in the Senate minority during Trump's time in office, the still-narrow odds of Democrats taking back that chamber have improved in recent weeks. If Blumenthal returns to chair the investigations subcommittee, it would grant him significantly greater powers to subpoena and control the agenda, and he's made it clear that crypto would be high on his list of topic areas. Prediction market Kalshi gives Democrats a 69% chance at the moment.

Blumenthal said the arrangements raise ethical and legal concerns, and Hines later became Tether's top U.S. executive. Tether said outside lawyers had conducted an internal investigation and found no evidence of wrongdoing.

title: Bitcoin, gold trim early losses as yen gives up gains. Oil stays near $100
article_text:
Bitcoin, gold trim early losses as yen gives up gains. Oil stays near $100. Bitcoin, gold trim early losses as yen gives up gains. Oil stays near $100
Bitcoin and gold pared early losses as the yen gave up gains and Asian stocks rebounded, though oil near $100 keeps inflation risks in focus.
- Bitcoin recovered to nearly $82,000 during Asian trading Friday as gold, Asian stocks and Nasdaq futures rebounded while the Japanese yen surrendered early gains.
- About $435 million in cryptocurrency futures positions were liquidated over 24 hours, including $385 million in bullish bets, as bitcoin tested its 50-day moving average.
- Persistently high oil prices and weak demand for spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which recorded $381 million in outflows Thursday, could limit a broader rally in risk assets.
Bitcoin 
The largest cryptocurrency by market value recovered to nearly $82,000 after hitting lows below $81,000 overnight, according to CoinDesk data. At the time of writing, bitcoin was testing its 50-day simple moving average, a widely followed gauge of near-term market momentum. Other cryptocurrencies, such as ether 
Crypto futures positions worth $435 million were liquidated over the past 24 hours, including $385 million in longs, a sign that leverage was skewed toward the bullish side.
Gold, a traditional haven asset, bounced back to $4,020 per ounce from an early low of $3,986, a level last seen on July 29.
Major Asian equity indices, including Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi, also rebounded from session lows. Nasdaq futures rose 0.17% to 29,190, up from 29,022 earlier in the day.
The risk-off tone had strengthened in early Asian trading as the yen climbed to 156.07 per U.S. dollar, its highest level since Sept. 18. Hotter-than-expected Japanese inflation data reinforced expectations of further Bank of Japan rate hikes, boosting the currency alongside a haven bid driven by AI-related jitters.
Yen moves often ripple through global markets because the currency has long been used to fund risk-on carry trades.
Those yen gains proved fleeting, however, with the currency quickly falling back toward 157 per U.S. dollar.
Whether the risk reset lasts may also depend on oil. WTI futures traded near $100, even after U.S. President Donald Trump invoked a Cold War-era law aimed at boosting fuel production. The move has yet to materially cool oil prices.
A sustained rise in oil could fuel global inflation and weigh on risk assets. Besides, a consistent demand for spot bitcoin ETFs is lacking for a steep price rally to materialize. On Thursday, these U.S.-listed funds lost $381 million in outflows, according to preliminary data from SoSoValue.
reference_summary: Bitcoin recovered to nearly $82,000 after falling below $81,000 overnight, while gold and Asian stocks also recovered as the Japanese yen gave up earlier gains. Gold rose back to about $4,020 an ounce, but oil remained near $100 a barrel, keeping inflation concerns in focus. Preliminary data showed U.S. bitcoin investment funds lost $381 million through withdrawals on Thursday, indicating weak demand despite the price rebound.

title: Ethereum delays Glamsterdam test after security devs flag risk to existing contracts
article_text:
Ethereum delays Glamsterdam test after security devs flag risk to existing contracts. Ethereum delays Glamsterdam test after security devs flag risk to existing contracts
Developers canceled Monday's Hoodi activation after researchers showed how new gas rules could let smart contracts permanently record failed operations.
- Ethereum developers postponed the Glamsterdam upgrade on the Hoodi test network after researchers found that proposed gas-accounting changes could alter how existing smart contracts handle failed transactions.
- ChainSecurity found that EIP-8037 and EIP-8038 could leave some contracts with more or less gas than expected, potentially making errors permanent or causing otherwise valid operations to fail.
- No replacement date has been announced for the Hoodi test or its planned 200 million gas limit, and Ethereum’s mainnet upgrade date remains unconfirmed.
Ethereum developers have called off Monday's Glamsterdam upgrade on the Hoodi test network after security researchers identified a problem that could change how existing smart contracts handle failed transactions, potentially allowing errors to become permanent.
The upgrade was due to activate on Oct. 26 at 17:42:48 UTC. Developers postponed it during Thursday's All Core Devs Execution meeting to investigate how a proposed change to Ethereum's gas accounting interacts with contracts already running on the main network.
No replacement date has been announced.
The concern centers on EIP-8037, which changes how Ethereum charges for creating new records in its database. The proposal is intended to limit the growth of that database as Ethereum increases the number of transactions its network can process.
Security firm ChainSecurity published an analysis on Oct. 13 showing that the change, combined with EIP-8038, could alter how contracts respond when another contract they call runs out of gas, or the fees used to pay the network’s operators.
Some contracts are designed to catch a failed operation and continue processing. They may record that an attempt failed, disable further attempts or move to another step. Developers sometimes rely on the remaining gas being too low for those actions to finish, causing the entire transaction to reverse instead.
Glamsterdam changes that calculation. Under the proposed rules, gas used to create certain records can be restored when those changes are undone. That can leave enough gas for a contract to complete a failure-handling operation that previously would have reversed.
There is also a risk in the opposite direction. ChainSecurity calculated that creating a new storage slot could require 110,020 gas when a separate allowance is exhausted, compared with 22,100 under the old rules. A contract using an existing gas budget might fail while carrying out an otherwise valid operation.
The findings concern how existing software would behave under proposed rules. ChainSecurity has demonstrated the mechanisms but has not publicly established that a major production protocol is exploitable.
Glamsterdam brings several changes to Ethereum, including a new system for choosing block builders and improvements intended to let the network handle larger blocks.
It completed its Sepolia testnet activation on Oct. 6. Hoodi was the next public rehearsal, alongside a planned increase in its gas limit to 200 million — which has also been postponed now.
Read more: Ethereum’s Glamsterdam test runs near 200 million gas per block after upgrade
Ethereum's mainnet has no confirmed Glamsterdam activation date, and the findings do not indicate that existing contracts are currently being exploited through these proposed changes.
reference_summary: Ethereum developers postponed the Glamsterdam upgrade's October 26 test on the Hoodi network after ChainSecurity researchers found that proposed changes to computing charges could disrupt existing transaction programs. The changes could make some failed operations leave permanent records or cause otherwise valid operations to fail. No replacement test date or main-network launch date is confirmed, and researchers have not established that a major live service can be exploited through the proposed changes.

title: Cardano holders are being asked to bet $5 million on copper hitting a new record
article_text:
Cardano holders are being asked to bet $5 million on copper hitting a new record. Cardano holders are being asked to bet $5 million on copper hitting a new record
Toto Finance wants 22 million ADA from Cardano’s treasury to buy tokenized copper, and the metal would have to trade well above its all-time high for holders to get their money back.
- Toto Finance is seeking 22 million ADA, or about $5 million, from Cardano’s treasury to buy and tokenize copper, with voting set to close Nov. 15.
- Copper would need to rise about 49.4% for the treasury to recover its investment if the full budget is spent and ADA’s dollar price remains unchanged.
- The proposal would use more than half of Cardano’s remaining withdrawal allowance, while Toto could receive up to 3.36 million ADA and retain commercial rights to its separately funded tokenized-copper business.
Cardano’s community treasury is being asked to spend about $5 million on a copper reserve, with costs that would require the metal to rise nearly 50% to recover the original investment under the proposal’s assumptions.
Toto Finance, a company that turns physical commodities into blockchain tokens, wants 22 million ADA for what it calls the Cardano Strategic Copper Reserve. Voting closes Nov. 15.
Copper, also known as “Dr. Copper” for its role as a barometer of global growth, is widely tracked as a signal of industrial expansion, with rising prices often pointing to an economic boom.
About two-thirds of the money would buy exchange-grade copper stored in a COMEX-approved warehouse near New Orleans. A token called CuTT would represent each verified pound. The metal would be held for 18 to 24 months, then sold over the following year, with net proceeds and unused funds returned to the treasury by month 36.
There is no guarantee the treasury gets its original ADA back.
The other third covers storage, insurance, audits, oversight and Toto’s work. If the full budget is spent and ADA’s dollar price stays unchanged, copper would need to rise about 49.4% to recover the withdrawal.
The proposal assumes copper is bought at $6.73 a pound and sold at about $10.06. Lower spending would reduce that hurdle, while a stronger ADA would raise it.
“Copper has significant upside potential, with bullish scenarios projecting approximately 30% annual appreciation. At that rate, copper would appreciate 69% over 24 months, potentially more than covering the 49.4% break-even threshold. Of course, commodity prices can also decline,” Monty Metzger, Toto’s founder and chairman, told CoinDesk in an email.
“Toto takes no profit from this proposal,” Metzger added, attributing much of the additional spending to Cardano’s constitutional requirements for oversight and auditing.
The budget allocates 2.64 million ADA to Toto for technology and project management, plus a 441,732 ADA execution fee. Toto could also receive up to 278,291 ADA through a margin on third-party storage and insurance invoices, included within the operating budget. Together, those payments could reach about 3.36 million ADA, roughly 15% of the request.
What Toto gets
Toto would retain the platform’s commercial rights and income from its separately funded CuTT business. The treasury’s financial return would come from its copper sales and unused funds.
Metzger said the company wants to scale the product to “$5 billion in tokenized copper assets” and that “Cardano could become our flagship showcase.”
The tokens would first be minted on Ethereum and locked in a bridge, software that allows matching tokens to be issued on Cardano. The contracts and their security reviews remain future work. Metzger said trackers of tokenized real-world assets have “historically focused heavily on Ethereum-based assets.”
Toto would hold legal title to the copper. Metzger said “an independent collateral agent and first-priority security arrangements” would protect the treasury if Toto failed, but did not name the agent.
The request lands with Cardano’s spending room nearly used up.
A 500 million ADA withdrawal cap runs through about July 2027, and 457.4 million had been used as of Oct. 16 — meaning the copper proposal would consume just over half the remaining allowance. Under the existing rules, returning the proceeds would not replenish it.
In late May, the Cardano Foundation’s 7.8 million ADA request for its 2026 summit won 65.21% support, short of the two-thirds required, and the event was canceled. Toto is asking for nearly three times as much.
Read More: Cardano Summit 2026 canceled after community votes against Foundation funding proposal
reference_summary: Toto Finance is asking Cardano's community treasury for 22 million ADA, worth about $5 million, to buy copper represented by digital tokens, with voting ending November 15. About two-thirds would buy metal and the rest would cover expenses, meaning copper would need to rise roughly 49.4% to recover the full investment if the entire budget is spent and ADA's dollar price stays unchanged. The proposal would use more than half of Cardano's remaining spending allowance, and repayment of the original ADA amount is not guaranteed.

title: Franklin Templeton adds $150 million in fund shares to XRP Ledger, all in one wallet
article_text:
Franklin Templeton adds $150 million in fund shares to XRP Ledger, all in one wallet. Franklin Templeton adds $150 million in fund shares to XRP Ledger, all in one wallet
Two subscriptions on Thursday nearly quadrupled the fund’s tokens on the network. The receiving wallet shares its authorized signers with the issuer.
- Franklin Templeton added about $150 million in shares of its tokenized money market fund to the XRP Ledger, bringing the network’s total to nearly 193 million shares worth about $200 million.
- All sgBENJI shares on the XRP Ledger remain in a single wallet that shares transaction signers with Franklin’s issuing account, though it is unclear whether the wallet represents one investor or multiple clients.
- The fund invests in short-term dollar debt and money-market instruments, and its XRP Ledger holdings can be approved, frozen or recovered by Franklin.
Franklin Templeton added $150 million worth of shares in its tokenized money market fund to the XRP Ledger earlier Friday, with every new share went to one wallet which now holds the fund’s entire token balance on the network.
That wallet and Franklin’s issuing account authorize the identical eight signing addresses. Any two can jointly approve a transaction, according to CoinDesk’s review of ledger records.
The wallet holds nearly 193 million sgBENJI shares, up from about 48 million before Thursday. At the $1.039 share price recorded in the transactions, that is worth about $200 million.
RWA.xyz ranks Franklin second in its XRP Ledger table of tokenized asset platforms, behind Ripple’s RLUSD stablecoin at about $930 million and ahead of Ondo at $185 million.
Each token represents a share of the Singapore-domiciled Franklin OnChain U.S. Dollar Short-Term Money Market Fund. It invests in short-term dollar debt and money-market instruments, including government paper, commercial paper and bank deposits. Returns accumulate in the share price.
On Wednesday, Franklin’s issuing account wrote two subscription receipts onto the ledger. Each recorded a $75 million cash subscription and carried its own reference code.
Two batches of just over 72,184,793 shares followed at 02:58 and 04:13 UTC Thursday, each carrying a matching receipt code and a $1.039 share price.
The receipts leave the investors, funding source and any connection to existing holdings on Stellar, the other blockchain the fund uses, undisclosed.
RWA.xyz lists Franklin’s XRP Ledger position at about $193 million, matching the share count at a dollar each. Thursday’s recorded share price puts its value nearly $8 million higher.
Why one wallet
Brokers and custodians routinely hold shares for many clients in one account, tracking individual ownership separately.
Franklin’s fund documents describe a register combining blockchain entries with records held outside the network, including information “which links the wallet addresses of the entries on the distributed ledger to their real-world identities.”
Whether this particular wallet represents one investor or several remains unclear.
CoinDesk asked Franklin whether it is an omnibus account, how many investors funded the subscriptions and whether they or their custodians will receive tokens in separate addresses. The firm had not responded as of Asia morning hours on Saturday.
Franklin and DBS announced the fund’s Singapore-authorized structure in November 2025 with a $20 minimum investment. Initially available to wealth and accredited clients, retail access was expected in early 2026.
Their September 2025 agreement with Ripple outlined plans for eligible DBS Digital Exchange clients to switch between sgBENJI and RLUSD. DBS also said it would explore lending against the fund tokens.
Holding sgBENJI directly on XRPL requires Franklin’s approval. Its settings also allow the issuer to freeze balances and recover tokens.
Thursday’s transactions nearly quadrupled the number of sgBENJI shares on the XRP Ledger. The number of wallets holding any of them stayed at one.

reference_summary: Franklin Templeton added about $150 million in digital shares of its short-term U.S. dollar investment fund to the XRP Ledger, bringing the network's total to nearly 193 million shares worth about $200 million. The fund invests in short-term debt and bank deposits, and each digital token represents a fund share. All the fund's digital shares on the network remain in one wallet, but it is unclear whether that wallet holds them for one investor or several clients.

title: Robinhood sees surge in bitcoin, gold prediction markets as traders move beyond sports
article_text:
Robinhood sees surge in bitcoin, gold prediction markets as traders move beyond sports. Robinhood sees surge in bitcoin, gold prediction markets as traders move beyond sports
The company's head of futures and prediction markets said bitcoin, gold and oil contracts are among its fastest-growing prediction markets.
- Bitcoin, gold and oil price contracts are among the fastest-growing prediction market products, according to Robinhood executive JB Mackenzie.
- The Federal Reserve's interest rate decision was Robinhood's largest event contract in September, while crypto contracts have moved toward 15-minute settlement periods.
- Prediction markets are also drawing customers into Robinhood's stock, crypto and retirement products, potentially making the business one of the company's fastest-growing segments.
Robinhood is seeing growing demand for prediction markets tied to bitcoin, gold and oil, as traders increasingly look beyond sports and elections to bet on moves in financial markets.
Price volatility contracts tied to those assets are among the fastest-growing products in prediction markets, according to JB Mackenzie, VP and GM for futures and prediction markets at Robinhood.
Sports is the largest product the platform offers, said Mackenzie at the NEXTPredict conference in New York on Thursday. However, he said there is a shift in how people use the platform.
"We've now started to see price volatility contracts, such as bitcoin, crude oil, gold, start to dominate the marketplace, and they're the fastest growing products that are out there," Mackenzie said.
Prediction markets allow traders to buy contracts based on whether an event will happen, with prices reflecting the market's implied probability of an outcome. A contract might ask whether bitcoin will trade above a certain price at a set time, giving traders a way to take a position without buying the cryptocurrency itself.
The market has grown from its roots in elections into sports, economic data and short-term price bets. Robinhood entered the business through a partnership with Kalshi, a federally regulated prediction market exchange, and has since made event contracts a growing part of its trading platform.
The expansion comes as sports contracts face legal challenges from state gambling regulators, raising questions about how much of that market will remain available.
Financial contracts could offer another source of growth.
Mackenzie said Robinhood's largest event contract in September wasn't tied to sports but to the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision, reflecting growing interest in economic events.
Traders are also moving toward shorter contracts, particularly in crypto, where some products now settle in as little as 15 minutes.
"It started off with a week. It's moved to a day, and now we're down to 15 [minutes]," he said.
Asked about the risks, he compared 15-minute crypto contracts to zero-day options, which expire on the same trading day. Both can produce rapid losses, though their structures differ.
For Robinhood, prediction markets are also becoming a way to bring customers into its other businesses. Mackenzie said users who arrive at the trade event contracts often begin exploring stocks, cryptocurrencies, futures and options. Some also discover the platform's individual retirement accounts.
"What you see them do is almost immediately start to build out into equities, crypto, futures, options," he said.
Robinhood has 11 businesses generating more than $100 million in annual revenue each, Mackenzie said, noting that prediction markets could be the company’s fastest-growing segment among them.
reference_summary: Robinhood executive JB Mackenzie said contracts letting customers bet on bitcoin, gold and oil prices are among its fastest-growing prediction-market products, although sports remains its largest category. These contracts pay according to whether an event happens, such as bitcoin exceeding a set price, without requiring users to buy the asset. The Federal Reserve's interest-rate decision was Robinhood's biggest event contract in September, and some cryptocurrency contracts now settle in just 15 minutes.

title: Bitcoin Core changes security rules as AI makes finding code bugs dangerously easy
article_text:
Bitcoin Core changes security rules as AI makes finding code bugs dangerously easy. Bitcoin Core changes security rules as AI makes finding code bugs dangerously easy
Developers merged a policy change that ends the months-long embargo for flaws a chatbot could rediscover, after a summer in which AI found hundreds of bitcoin bugs before the humans did.
- Bitcoin Core will quickly disclose and patch vulnerabilities that can be found with a simple prompt to an artificial intelligence model, replacing embargoes that could last about a year.
- Maintainers said the change would speed fixes for easily rediscovered flaws, though updates may receive less testing before reaching users.
- The policy follows a surge in AI-assisted security reports, including a review of 390 Bitcoin projects that identified 4,962 potential flaws, 85 of them critical.
Bitcoin Core, the software most of the bitcoin network runs on, will stop sitting on bug fixes for months when the bug is one an AI could find again, after its maintainers merged a change to the project’s security policy on Thursday.
Core previously graded every reported vulnerability by severity and timed disclosure accordingly. Low-severity flaws were revealed two weeks after the next major version shipped. Medium and high ones stayed under embargo until two weeks after the last affected version reached end of life.
The logic was that shipping a fix quietly and explaining it much later kept attackers from learning about a hole before the people running nodes, the computers that check and relay every bitcoin transaction, had upgraded.
But the old rule was built for a world where finding a bug took skill, and the spread of AI tools has broken how that process worked.
“We recently experienced an increase in the number of reports for security vulnerabilities that can be easily (re-)discovered,” Antoine Poinsot, the Chaincode Labs developer who wrote the change, said in his proposal.
“This is largely due to LLMs drastically reducing the bar to find certain classes of issues or identify covert fixes.”
How it works
Core can now flag a bug as easy to discover during triage, which in practice means one that “can be found with a simple prompt to an LLM.” Those bugs get a fix copied back to every version Core still supports, shipped in a point release “as soon as possible” along with a security advisory carrying some details.
“For these issues that are easy to find, this is the wrong tradeoff,” the policy reads of the old embargo. “The embargo period achieves little but it delays the availability of a fixed release.”
Fixes “won’t have as much ‘bake time’” in testing before they reach users, however, Poinsot wrote.
Not every developer agreed on how far to go. Antoine Riard, a longtime bitcoin security researcher, wanted Core to keep the option of shipping a fix without an advisory and holding the details back case by case.
Poinsot refused. “Alerting users of a security vulnerability without any details could create more risk unnecessarily,” he wrote, pointing to “a rushed migration by users who would otherwise not be affected.”
A volunteer group of 16 developers calling itself the Bitcoin Red Team ran AI models across 390 bitcoin projects in about a day in late July and logged 4,962 findings, with 85 of them critical.
Within days a BTCPay Server flaw the group had reported privately was being exploited on live merchant servers. The attacks drained the Lightning nodes merchants use to take small bitcoin payments. Core Lightning, one of the main Lightning implementations, told operators to disconnect after AI-generated reports to its small team turned out to be real.
A bigger loss came from a bug no AI needed to find. A flaw in Coldcard hardware-wallet firmware, dormant since 2021, let attackers drain 594 BTC in 25 minutes on July 30, and losses neared $114 million across four sweeps. When Coldcard shipped its fix, it said AI had helped catch more bugs along the way.
No bug has been flagged under the new rule yet, but a secret any model can regenerate in one prompt was never going to protect users for long.
reference_summary: Bitcoin Core developers changed their security policy to release fixes and disclose details quickly when a software flaw can be rediscovered with a simple AI request. The change replaces delays that could last months, aiming to protect users sooner, although developers acknowledge that fixes may receive less testing before release. No vulnerability has yet been designated under the new rule.

title: Bitcoin's price is as jumpy as Nvidia's and eight times more turbulent than the euro
article_text:
Bitcoin's price is as jumpy as Nvidia's and eight times more turbulent than the euro. Bitcoin's price is as jumpy as Nvidia's and eight times more turbulent than the euro
Your day-ahead look for Oct. 23, 2026
This is an excerpt from CoinDesk newsletter 'Daybook.' Sign up here, if you haven't already.
Earlier this week, CoinDesk discussed how risk management in bitcoin is becoming increasingly popular, steadily reducing the the largest cryptocurrency’s volatility and making it more palatable to professional investors.
That raises a question. How does its stability compare with major assets such as gold, its traditional rival, with the S&P 500, the biggest stock index, with the euro-dollar exchange rate, the most liquid fiat currency pair, and with Nvidia 
It transpires there is still a long way to go before bitcoin can match the euro-dollar, gold and stock indexes in terms of stability.
That’s according to a widely tracked metric called realized volatility, which measures how much an asset's price has moved over a period, such as 30 or 90 days. The gauge is the standard deviation of daily returns, usually annualized to show what a full year of such moves would look like. The higher the number, the bigger the swings and the stronger the perception that the asset is risky.
Bitcoin's 90-day realized volatility stood at about 38% as of Thursday, based on CoinDesk's calculations. Its main rival, gold, is at about 23.5%. The S&P 500 sits at about 11%, so bitcoin is a little over three times as jumpy as stocks.
EUR/USD, which matches the euro — the shared currency of 21 countries — against the dollar, the global reserve currency, is the steadiest of all, with a 90-day realized volatility of 4.6%. Bitcoin is roughly eight times as volatile.
The currency pair’s volatility has stayed in single digits despite uncertainty over the French government debt and the resulting recent slide in the euro. Most fiat currency pairs have realized volatility below 10%.
That shows just how much ground BTC, despite its limited-supply feature, has to cover before it can rival traditional medium of exchanges and validate the bitcoin maximalists' view that crypto is better than paper currencies.
The closest match is Nvidia at about 37%. Bitcoin and the AI bellwether now swing by almost the same amount.
The broader improvement in bitcoin, however, is clear. The cryptocurrency’s 90-day volatility has averaged about 58% since January 2020 and peaked at 134% in June 2020. Its calmest reading of 27.5% came in September 2025 when prices rose above $100,000.
So bitcoin has settled down a lot, and it now moves like a big tech stock. But it has yet to rival a national currency. Stay alert!

Today’s signal
The chart on the left shows BVIV, which is Volmex’s 30-day bitcoin implied volatility index, a gauge of options-based expectations for price turbulence in the largest cryptocurrency over four weeks.
On the right is the VIX index, which shows expected volatility in the S&P 500 index.
As of now, the VIX has topped its 200-day moving average, a sign traders are pricing increased uncertainty and wider price swings in the index. On the other hand, BVIV remains below its 200-day average, pointing to expectations for relative stability in the crypto market.
How long bitcoin can defy a potential volatility explosion on Wall Street remains to be seen.
reference_summary: CoinDesk's comparison of daily price changes over 90 days found bitcoin's price about as jumpy as Nvidia shares, with swings more than three times those of the S&P 500 stock index and about eight times those of the euro against the dollar. Bitcoin's price swings have declined compared with their average since 2020, but remain larger than those of gold and major national currencies.

title: Live updates: Bitcoin holds above $81,000 as oil prices hit six-month high

Live updates: Bitcoin holds above $81,000 as oil prices hit six-month high. Yesterday’s 19 basis point slide in the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield was the largest one-day move downward since March 2023, when the failure of Silicon Valley Bank had investors worried about a domino effect across the country.
Markets having calmed for the moment — the Nasdaq and S&P 500 are about flat on Friday, and French bond spreads (to Germany) are little changed — yields are cautiously edging higher.
The U.S. 10-year yield is up 4.3 basis points to 4.994%, and the 2-year yield is up 6 basis points to 4.695%.
Next week brings the Federal Reserve’s policy meeting, and investors continue to overwhelmingly bet the central bank leaves its benchmark fed funds rate unchanged.
Gold fell below $4,000 an ounce for the first time since July, trading around $3,990, roughly 30% below its January all-time high of $5,600. Silver has dropped more than 2% over the past 24 hours to around $53.40 an ounce, leaving it 56% below its January record high.
Good news is bad news as the AI trade continues to struggle. Bloom Energy (BE) shares fell 10% in U.S. trading on Friday despite beating revenue and earnings expectations on Thursday. Third-quarter revenue rose 138% year over year to $1.24 billion, exceeding forecasts of $1.07 billion, while adjusted earnings per share reached $0.94, ahead of the $0.67 expected.
Even with yesterday’s ugly action included, bitcoin BTC$77,907.06 has gained about 39% over the nearly four months since it sat just below $59,000 on July 1.
One trader crunched the numbers. Since July 1, there have been 2,724 hourly candles, and the 15 strongest candles — just 0.55% — produced enough gains for that entire 39% advance.
Removing the 20 strongest hours over the last four months, and bitcoin would have actually dropped 6.8%.
“This is exactly why going fully cash and waiting for the ‘perfect entry’ is so dangerous,” the trader concluded. “Bitcoin could spend weeks doing absolutely nothing and deliver the entire rally while you are waiting to buy lower.”
Bitcoin ETFs had largest outflows since June; history says outlook isn't good
The U.S.-listed spot bitcoin ETF suffered $635 million in outflows during yesterday’s panicky action, according to Farside Investors. That’s the largest daily outflow since June 25.
While the contrarian take might be, “fantastic, the leveraged, fast-money types were flushed out, and now we’re poised to move higher,” history suggests otherwise.
According to Farside, bitcoin has tended to perform poorly in the days and weeks following outsized outflows. For instances of outflows greater than $300 million (there have been 22 such days prior to yesterday), bitcoin, on average, was significantly lower 7, 30, and 90 days later.
The caveat, of course, is that history is quite limited, given the ETFs have been around for less than three years, and is also likely skewed by the bear market begun in October 2025.
Bitcoin goes quiet near $81,500 after a week of $3,000 swings
Bitcoin dipped to about $81,000 late Thursday and has since spent the day boxed in a range of less than $1,000, trading near $81,500 early Friday. After a week of $3,000 swings, it’s the calmest stretch bitcoin has had in days.
It’s down 0.4% over 24 hours and still sits below $82,500, the support it lost on Thursday.
Altcoins were mixed. BNB was the standout, up nearly 2% to about $745, and DOGE added about 1%. XMR gave back part of Thursday’s jump, falling 7% to about $607, and ZEC lost nearly 4% to about $1,200. HYPE, XRP, ether and SOL slipped about 1% or less, with ether just under $2,400, according to CoinDesk data.
Stocks found their footing too. Nasdaq 100 futures were little changed after the index’s worst day since June, and an ETF tracking chipmakers edged higher before the open. Meta kept falling, while SpaceX climbed on reports that it plans to become a wireless carrier.
Oil is the worry. Brent crude touched its highest level since early May, which complicates the inflation outlook heading into the Fed’s Oct. 27–28 meeting. Treasuries gave back some of Thursday’s haven rally, which had pushed the 10-year yield down by the most in more than a year. Gold and the dollar were flat.
reference_summary: Bitcoin steadied near $81,500 on Friday after large swings earlier in the week, while U.S. stock markets were broadly flat. U.S. funds holding bitcoin lost $635 million through withdrawals the previous day, their largest daily outflow since June 25, according to Farside Investors. Brent oil reached its highest level since early May, complicating the inflation outlook before the Federal Reserve's October 27–28 meeting.

title: Bitcoin appears to have decoupled from midterm cycle bottom history
article_text:
Bitcoin appears to have decoupled from midterm cycle bottom history. Bitcoin appears to have decoupled from midterm cycle bottom history
Previous bitcoin bear-market lows followed U.S. midterms, but this year’s recovery raises the possibility that the bottom arrived months earlier.
- Bitcoin reached major bear-market lows shortly after the 2014, 2018 and 2022 midterm elections, but this year’s low came 125 days before Election Day.
- Bitcoin recovered about 40% from its July 1 low of $57,850 to roughly $81,455 on Oct. 22, despite falling about 6% over the past 30 days.
- Bitcoin’s recurring weakness around midterms appears more closely tied to its own market cycles than to elections, as technology stocks have shown a less consistent pattern.
U.S. midterm elections are just 10 days away and bitcoin 
Bitcoin bottomed in January 2015, December 2018 and November 2022, shortly after the preceding midterms. Those lows arrived approximately 71, 38 and 13 days after election day, respectively.
This year, bitcoin’s lowest price so far came much earlier. Bitcoin touched $57,850 on July 1, some 125 days before the Nov. 3 election. By Oct. 22, the price had recovered to around $81,455, roughly 40% above that low.
Historical returns also reveal substantial weakness over the broader pre-election period. Bitcoin fell approximately 29% in the six months before the 2018 midterms and 37% before the 2022 vote.
Technology stocks have also experienced weakness around midterms. The Invesco QQQ Trust fell roughly 23% from the end of September to its December 2018 low, with much of the decline occurring after election day. It also dropped 17% in the three months preceding the 2022 vote. However, QQQ gained 17% over the six months before the 2014 midterms, showing the pattern is not entirely consistent.
Bitcoin and QQQ are both down roughly 6% over the past 30 days. Over 90 days, however, bitcoin remained up 26%, compared with QQQ’s 3% gain. QQQ’s pullback followed an all-time high of $762.86 on Oct. 6.
The comparison suggests bitcoin’s historical midterm weakness reflects its own market cycles more consistently than an election effect.
reference_summary: Bitcoin's recovery has raised the possibility that this year's lowest price came before the U.S. midterm elections, unlike major lows following the 2014, 2018 and 2022 elections. It rose about 40% from $57,850 on July 1 to roughly $81,455 on October 22, with the July low occurring 125 days before Election Day. The article suggests the historical pattern is linked more closely to bitcoin's own market cycles than to the elections themselves.

title: Sweden’s central bank revives e-krona debate as stablecoins and digital euro loom
article_text:
Sweden’s central bank revives e-krona debate as stablecoins and digital euro loom. Sweden’s central bank revives e-krona debate as stablecoins and digital euro loom
The Riksbank sees an e-krona as critical to securing national payments and monetary control.
- Sweden’s central bank warns foreign stablecoins and a digital euro risk eroding krona demand.
- The Riksbank sees an e-krona as critical to securing national payments and monetary control.
- Lawmakers have yet to approve the e-krona, which would take at least five years to launch.
Sweden’s central bank is calling for lawmakers to reconsider a digital krona, warning that foreign-currency stablecoins and a planned digital euro could erode the currency’s role in payments.
An e-krona would give the public access to central bank money in digital form. A 2023 government inquiry found too little need for one, but the Riksbank says changes in how people pay and growing security risks may warrant a new review.
“If our cash becomes digital and Swedish kronor are not available in a usable digital form, then the krona may not be able to compete with other, more convenient digital payment instruments that can easily be used across borders,” Deputy Governor Per Jansson told Reuters on the sidelines of a conference.
The Riksbank hasn’t taken a position on issuing one, but wants lawmakers to start preparing legislation now, since the work would take at least five years.
The central bank warned that stablecoins tied to foreign currencies could reduce demand for the krona in a recent letter. It sees little near-term risk but says the long-term threat remains.
Cash use has fallen sharply in the country. Just 5% of Swedes surveyed used cash for their last purchase, according to Riksbank data cited in the report, and a shift away from the krona could make it harder for the bank to steer the economy and protect financial stability.
The Riksbank also sees an e-krona as a backup payment option during power or telecom outages, with offline payments among its potential features.
Sweden could draw on the digital euro’s infrastructure to build the system, with that central bank digital currency potentially debuting in 2029 if EU lawmakers approved the required rules.
reference_summary: Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, wants lawmakers to reconsider an e-krona, a digital form of money issued directly by the central bank for public use. It warns that foreign-currency stablecoins and a planned digital euro could reduce use of the Swedish krona and weaken its control over the economy and national payments. The bank has not decided whether to issue an e-krona, and preparing a launch would take at least five years.
